en: The Profound Meaning of the Contemplation Sutra, Fascicle One, Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shandao. Part One:
The Profound Meaning of the Contemplation Sutra. First, Exhorting the Great Assembly to Make Vows and Take Refuge in the Triple Gem.
The assembly of monastics and laypeople alike each gave rise to the unsurpassed resolve;
birth and death are most difficult to weary of, and the Buddha-dharma is likewise difficult to rejoice in.
Together, we shall give rise to adamantine resolve and transcend horizontally to sever the four currents.
Vowing to enter the realm of Amitābha, I take refuge and pay homage with palms joined.
World-Honored One, with a single mind, I take refuge in all the Buddhas throughout the ten directions—
the Buddhas of the Dharma-nature, True Suchness, and the Reward and Transformation bodies.
Each and every Bodhisattva’s body, with retinues as infinite as the sea,
In their adornments and transformations, throughout the oceans of the ten stages and the three levels of worthiness,
Whether their time and kalpas are fulfilled or not, whether their wisdom and practice are perfected or not—
Whether the [delusions] are exhausted or not yet exhausted, whether habitual tendencies have perished or not yet perished,
whether there is effort or no effort, whether it is realized wisdom or not yet realized wisdom,
whether it be wondrous enlightenment or equal enlightenment, and the state of samādhi within the adamantine mind— [All these are encompassed therein.]
Following a single moment of correspondence, those who attain the fruition of virtue and nirvana—
we all take refuge in them, the Three Buddhas, Honored Ones of Bodhi.
Through the power of unimpeded supernormal faculties, may you secretly bestow your grace and grant us your protection.
We all take refuge in the noble ones of the three vehicles,
who have trained in the Buddha’s heart of great compassion and never wavered for a long time.
We pray that you will grant your protection from afar, so that in every thought-moment we may behold all the Buddhas.
We, with our ignorant bodies, have wandered through kalpas since time immemorial;
now we encounter the traces left by Śākyamuni Buddha during the final dharma-age,
the fundamental vows of Amitābha, and the essential gateway to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Through dedication whether in meditative concentration or distraction, may one swiftly realize the body of non-arising.
Relying upon the Bodhisattva Piṭaka and the ocean of the sudden teaching of the One Vehicle,
I speak these verses in homage to the Triple Gem, in accord with the Buddha-mind.
The Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, With their six supernormal powers, perceive and know me;
Now, following the teachings of the Two Honored Ones, I shall widely open the gate to the Pure Land.
I vow that by these merits, I shall bestow them equally upon all beings.
Having likewise resolved upon the Bodhi-mind, one shall be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Within this single fascicle of the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, I shall first provide a critical analysis in seven sections, and thereafter explain the meaning according to the text.

First, the preliminary presentation of the title; second, the subsequent explanation of its name; third, the interpretation of the meaning according to the text, along with a discernment of the different doctrines regarding the Great and Small Vehicles; fourth, the formal revelation of the distinctions among the speakers; fifth, the analytical determination of the differences between the two types of goodness—concentrated and dispersed—as well as their common and specific aspects; sixth, the reconciliation of contradictions between the sutras and treatises through an extensive application of questions and answers to dispel doubts; and seventh, the analytical determination of the extent of the benefits obtained by Vaidehī upon hearing the Buddha’s correct teaching.
First, regarding the preliminary indication of the title:

I humbly observe that True Suchness (Tathatā) is so vast that the five vehicles cannot fathom its limits; the Dharma-nature (Dharmatā) is so profound and sublime that even the ten stages of sages cannot exhaust its boundaries.
The substance and measure of True Suchness do not transcend the nature of the bustling mind; the boundless nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is, in its essential body, fundamentally unmoving.
In the dustless Dharma-realm, ordinary beings and sages are equally perfected; the suchness of the two defilements universally encompasses all sentient beings.

The merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are quiescent in their function and profound in their stillness; yet, because they are shrouded by the veil of defilements, the pure essence has no means to manifest its illumination. Thus, Great Compassion remained hidden during the transformation in the West, where he entered the gate of the burning house with a start, sprinkling nectar to moisten all living beings and brandishing the torch of wisdom to brighten the dense darkness of the eternal night.

The three types of giving (*dāna*) and so forth are fully prepared, and the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are collectively gathered; thus, the causes of suffering throughout long kalpas are revealed and shown, while the fruits of eternal bliss are awakened to and entered.

It is not that the natures of the deluded masses are separated or their desires different, such that there is no single true capacity [for enlightenment]; rather, all equally possess the utility of the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*). This enables the compassionate clouds to be spread across the triple world and the rain of Dharma to be poured down through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

There is none who does not equally partake in the cessation of worldly toil and universally receive the benefit of what was previously unheard; by this means, the seeds of Bodhi sprout from their core, and the shoots of perfect enlightenment grow and flourish in every thought-moment.

Based on the mind, one gives rise to sublime practices through eighty-four thousand gateways; whether gradual or sudden, each accords with what is appropriate, so that those who follow these conditions all attain liberation.

However, sentient beings have heavy obstructions, and those who seek awakening find it difficult to clarify their understanding. Although there are many gates through which they may be taught and benefited, ordinary delusions prevent them from grasping them all at once. Having encountered the cause for Vaidehī’s request, she now says: "I wish to be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss; I only pray that the Tathāgata will teach me how to contemplate and teach me right concentration."

Nevertheless, because the Master of Transformation of the Sahā world was so entreated, he extensively expounded the essential gateways to the Pure Land, revealing the vast vows of his distinct intention for the sake of those capable of attaining peace and bliss.
The essential gateways are precisely these two—the meditative and the non-meditative—found in this *Contemplation Sūtra*.

"Meditative" refers to calming the mind by stilling discursive thoughts; "non-meditative" refers to abandoning evil and cultivating goodness. One turns these two practices toward the aspiration for rebirth in the Pure Land.

Regarding the "vast vow," as stated in the *Mahā-sūtra*, among all ordinary beings—whether virtuous or non-virtuous—who attain birth [in that land], there are none who do not rely upon the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) of Amitābha Buddha’s great power of vows and karma.

Furthermore, the Buddha’s profound and subtle intention is vast and deep; his teachings are difficult to comprehend. Even the Three Sages and Ten Holy Ones cannot fathom their depths, let alone one like me, a mere stray hair outside the fold of faith, who would dare claim to know their essential meaning?
Looking upward, we reflect that Śākyamuni dispatches us from this world, while Amitābha welcomes us from that land. Since he calls out and he sends us forth, how could we not go?
We need only apply our minds with diligence to the Dharma, making the end of our lives our goal; once we cast off this defiled body, we shall immediately realize the eternal bliss of that Dharmatā.
This concludes the brief presentation of the title of the preface.
Second, regarding the subsequent explanation of the name:
the scripture states, *The Scripture on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha*, in one fascicle.
The term "Buddha" (Fo) is the correct phonetic transcription from the Western Land [India].
In this land, it is translated as "Awakened" (Jue). Because he has awakened himself and awakened others, and because his practice of awakening has reached ultimate fulfillment, he is named Buddha.

The term "self-awakening" distinguishes [the Bodhisattva] from ordinary beings; this is because Śrāvakas are narrow-minded and inferior, being able to benefit only themselves while lacking the great compassion that benefits others.

The term "awakening others" distinguishes [the Bodhisattva] from those of the two vehicles; this is because Bodhisattvas possess wisdom and are thus able to benefit themselves, and possess compassion and are thus able to benefit others, constantly practicing both compassion and wisdom in tandem, without clinging to existence or non-existence.

Regarding the phrase "awakening, practice, and fulfillment": this distinguishes [the Buddha] from the bodhisattvas. Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom-practice has already reached its limit and his kalpas have already been fulfilled, he has transcended the three stages; therefore, he is called a Buddha.
Regarding "discourse" (*yanshuo*): it is called discourse because it is articulated through vocal sounds.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma in response to various capacities is manifold and diverse; it is gradual or sudden according to what is appropriate, and there are differences in its concealment or manifestation. Sometimes it is taught through the six sense faculties, and the same applies to the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Responding to thoughts and following conditions, all receive its transformative benefit.
To say "Immeasurable Life" (Wúliàngshòu) is the Chinese pronunciation for this land.
To say "Namo Amituofo" is the authentic pronunciation of the Western Country.

Furthermore, "Nan" means "to take refuge," "Mu" means "life," "A" means "immeasurable," "Mi" means "limit," "Tuo" means "life," and "Fo" means "awakening. Therefore, it is said: "I take refuge in the life of Immeasurable Awakening."
This is a correspondence between the Sanskrit and the Chinese, and its meaning is as follows:
"Immeasurable Life" (Amitāyus) refers to the Dharma, while "Awakened One" (Buddha) refers to the person; since both the person and the Dharma are manifested together, he is named Amitābha Buddha.
Furthermore, it is said that "persons and dharmas" refer to the objects of contemplation,
which are twofold: first,
the retributive environment (*pariṇāmanirvṛtti*), and second, the primary retribution (*mūlanirvṛtti*).
Within the environment of retribution, there are three aspects:
first, the adornments beneath the earth, which include all jeweled banners whose radiance illuminates one another, and so forth.
Second is the adornment of the ground, which consists of all jewel grounds, ponds, groves, jeweled palaces, towers, and pavilions.
Third is the adornment of space, which consists of all manifested jewel palaces, flower nets, jewel clouds, transformed birds, and the sounds of music stirred up by the wind and light.
Although there were three types of distinctions as previously described, all are the sublime marks of the untainted reality of Amitābha’s Pure Land.
This concludes the summary of the adornments of the environment (*pratiṣṭhā-vibhūṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding what is called "dependent retribution" (niṣyanda-phala): from the contemplation of the sun down to the contemplation of the flower seat, this collectively clarifies dependent retribution.
Within this dependent retribution, there are both general and specific aspects.
Regarding the term "distinctive": the single visualization of the lotus seat is its specific basis, belonging exclusively to Amitābha Buddha.

The remaining six visualizations above are its general basis; they pertain to both ordinary beings and sages within the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). They are called "general" because all who attain birth therein may equally enjoy them.
Furthermore, within these six, there are both the real and the provisional.

Regarding the provisional: the perception of fire, the perception of water, and the perception of ice are their provisional bases, because they are objective appearances that resemble [their respective elements] as perceived within this realm.
Regarding the term "true basis" (satyāśraya): from the lapis lazuli ground down to the jeweled pavilions, this constitutes the true basis.
This is because it is the realm of truly non-outflowing (anāsrava) visible phenomena within that land.
Second, within the primary retribution (*vipāka*), there are also two aspects:
first, the adornment of the principal figure, which is Amitābha Buddha;
second, the adornment of the holy assembly, which consists of those currently present in that realm as well as those born together with him throughout the Dharma-realm of the ten directions.
Furthermore, within this primary retribution (*vipāka*), there is both the general and the specific.
As for the specific, it refers to Amitābha Buddha; within this specific category as well, there is both the real and the provisional.
Regarding the term "provisional primary retribution," this refers precisely to the eighth stage, the Contemplation of the Image.

The same applies to Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and others. Because sentient beings have heavy obstructions and their afflictions are deeply rooted, the Buddha feared that if they were to suddenly contemplate the true form, it would have no means of manifesting. Therefore, he caused provisional images of the true forms to be established so that one might dwell upon them with the mind; since these are identical to those Buddhas for the purpose of realizing the objective realm, they are called "provisional primary retribution."
What is called the "true retribution" refers precisely to the ninth stage, the contemplation of the true body (*dharmakāya*).

This arises from the preceding stages of the provisional and the correct; as one gradually stills distracted thoughts and the eye of the mind opens, one gains a coarse vision of the various adornments of the two types of pure retribution in that realm, thereby eliminating delusion and confusion. Because these obstructions are removed, one is able to perceive the characteristics of that true reality.
Regarding the statement "pervading the primary retribution," this refers to the assembly of the Holy One [Avalokiteśvara] and those below.
What was previously described as the pervasive and the specific, the true and the provisional, precisely clarifies the two types of retribution: the environment and the primary body.

"Contemplation" (*kan*) means illumination. One should constantly use the hands of pure faith to hold the radiance of wisdom, illuminating such matters as the primary reliance upon Amitābha. "Sutra" (*kyō*) means a warp;

just as a warp can hold the woof to form a bolt of cloth that serves its practical purpose, so too can the sutra uphold the Dharma, ensuring that principle and phenomenon correspond, and that the meaning remains intact whether one is in a state of meditative concentration or distraction according to one's capacity. It enables those who practice and aspire to rely necessarily upon the conditions and causes of teaching and practice, so that they may, by virtue of their vows, attain rebirth and realize the unconditioned bliss of the Dharma.

Having been born in that land, one has nothing further to fear; for a long duration, one practices until the fruit of supreme enlightenment is attained. The Dharma-body is eternally abiding, comparable to space; because it can bring about these benefits, it is called a "sūtra."

Regarding the term "one fascicle": although this single work, the *Contemplation Sūtra*, is said to consist of two formal assemblies of the primary teaching, it forms a single whole; therefore, it is called "one fascicle.
Thus, it is titled *The Buddha-Spoken Sūtra of the Contemplation of Immeasurable Life*, in one fascicle.
This concludes the explanation of the meaning of its name.
Third, regarding the differentiation and explanation of the differences between the various schools' tenets and the Great and Small Vehicles:
for instance, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* takes inconceivable liberation as its central tenet.
Just as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* takes the wisdom of emptiness as its primary tenet, there are many such examples;
likewise, this present *Contemplation Sūtra* takes the samādhi of contemplating the Buddha as its primary tenet, and it also takes the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha as its primary tenet.
Its essence consists of the single-minded aspiration for rebirth in the Pure Land.
Regarding the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles of the teachings, a question is asked:
"Within the two baskets (piṭaka) of the scriptures, to which basket does this sutra belong?"
"Between the two teachings, which teaching does it belong to?
He replied:
"This present *Amitābha Sūtra* is subsumed under the Bodhisattva Piṭaka and categorized within the Sudden Teaching."
4. Regarding the distinctions among those who preach:
Generally, the arising of all sūtras does not exceed five types:

first, the preaching of the Buddha; second, the preaching of noble disciples; third, the preaching of celestial seers; fourth, the preaching of spirits and deities; and fifth, the preaching of emanations.
Now, this *Amitābha Sūtra* (Contemplation Sūtra) was spoken by the Buddha himself.
A question is asked:
"In what place did the Buddha speak it?"
"For whom was it spoken? He replied,
"The Buddha spoke it in the royal palace for Vaidehī and others."
V. A detailed analysis of the two gates of concentration and distraction consists of six parts:
first, clarifying that the requester is Vaidehī;
second, clarifying that the one requested is the World-Honored One.
The first three illuminations (vidyā) that can expound are the Tathāgata;
the fourth illumination that is expounded consists of the two types of goodness—concentrated and dispersed—the sixteen contemplation gates;
and the fifth illumination that can act as the agent is the Tathāgata.
Sixth, those for whose sake [the teaching was given] are Vimalakīrti and others.
Question:
"Between the two types of goodness—concentrated and dispersed—who requested them?"
He replied:
"The single gate of meditative goodness was requested by Vaidehī; the single gate of non-meditative goodness was spoken by the Buddha himself. He asked:
"Unquestionably, in what texts do the two types of goodness—concentrated and dispersed—appear?
Now that the teachings are complete and not in vain, what kind of practitioner is capable of receiving them?
The answer is as follows:
"Explanation has two meanings.
First, those who slander the Dharma and lack faith, as well as those in the eight difficult circumstances or non-human beings—these do not receive [the teaching].
They are like withered forests or stubborn stones; there can be no expectation of them ever becoming moistened with life."
These sentient beings certainly lack the capacity for transformation through the teaching.

Apart from these, however, those who with single-minded faith and joy seek rebirth—whether exhausting their entire lives at the upper limit or maintaining ten recitations at the lower limit—will all, without exception, go there by virtue of the Buddha’s power of vows.
This concludes the answer to the previous question regarding which faculties are capable of receiving [the teaching].
Second, as for where this is stated in the texts, there are both general and specific references.
Regarding the general references, there are three distinct meanings.

What are they? First, from the passage where Vaidhī says to the Buddha, "I only pray that you will extensively explain for me the place free from sorrow and affliction," this is Vaidhī expressing her own intention as a general request for what she seeks.

2. Regarding the passage, "I only pray that the Buddha-sun will teach me how to contemplate the locus of pure karma," this refers to Vaidehī’s general request for the removal of [her] karmic hindrances.
Third, from the passage "The World-Honored One manifested the lands from the Light-Pavilion," he fulfills his previous general request for a detailed exposition on my behalf.
Although there are three distinct meanings [within this section], the response to the preceding general request is now complete.
Regarding the term "distinct," there are two meanings:

first, from the passage, "Vaidhī said to the Buddha: 'I now wish to be born in the world of Ultimate Bliss, in the presence of Amitābha Buddha,'" this refers to Vaidhī herself making a distinct selection of her own sought-after goal.
Second, regarding the passage "I only pray that you will teach me how to contemplate and teach me right concentration," this refers to Vaidehī herself requesting instruction on specific practices.
Although there are two different meanings, the response to the former [request] has now been concluded.
From this point forward, the following provides the answers regarding the meanings of the two gates: concentration (*samādhi*) and dispersion (*vikṣepa*).
Question: "What is meant by 'wholesome [states] of concentration' (*samāhita-kuśala*)?"
"What is meant by 'scattered goodness' (viprakīrṇakuśala)? He replied:
"From the Contemplation of the Sun down to the thirteenth contemplation and below is called 'concentrated goodness' (samāhitakuśala)."
"The three blessings and nine grades are called 'scattered goodness' (dispersed merit). He asked:
"What are the distinctions among the 'concentrated goodness' (meditative merit)?"
"In what text does this appear?
He replied, "As for where it appears, the Sūtra says: 'Instruct me in contemplation; instruct me in right concentration. This is the passage."
Regarding the distinction of "discrimination," there are two meanings:
first, contemplation; second, correct reception.

As for "contemplation," it refers to the preparatory practices (*pūrvayoga*) of observation, wherein one reflects upon the general and specific characteristics of the two types of retribution—the environment and the inhabitants—of that land.

The passage in the *Dìguān* (Contemplation of the Ground) states: "One who possesses such a perception is said to have a coarse vision of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This corresponds to the preceding phrase: "Instruct me in contemplation."

Regarding the term "right reception" (*samyaksamādhi*): when conceptualization and mental activity have completely ceased and all discursive thoughts have vanished, being in accord with *samādhi* is called "right reception.

This corresponds to the passage in the "Contemplation of the Grounds" which states, "If one attains *samādhi*, one sees the ground of that land clearly and distinctly," which aligns with the aforementioned phrase, "Instruct me in right reception."
Although there are two distinct meanings regarding meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*), this concludes the general response to the preceding question.
"Furthermore, my previous interpretation differs from that of other masters.
Those masters take the single phrase 'contemplation' (*manasikāra*) to correspond with the three blessings and nine grades as 'scattered goodness' (*vikṣiptakuśala*)."
To take a single phrase of "right reception" (samyak-samādhi) and apply it universally to encompass all sixteen contemplations as the "wholesome concentration" (dhyāna-kuśala)—
if one interprets it in this way, it would seem incorrect. Why?
As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"Contemplative absorption (*samāpatti*) is merely another name for samādhi," which is identical to the text concerning the contemplation of this stage.
Based on this textual evidence, how could it be understood as referring to mundane wholesome states (*pr̥thagjana-kuśala*)?

Furthermore, in the preceding passage, Vaidehī’s initial request was simply: "Teach me to contemplate the pure realms of action (*viśuddha-karma-sthāna*). Subsequently, she further requested: "Teach me to contemplate right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). Although there were these two requests, they refer exclusively to meditative wholesome states (*samāhita-kuśala*).
Furthermore, in the textual passages concerning miscellaneous wholesome deeds (*vyavakīrṇa-kuśala*), there is no place for a formal request; rather, it is the Buddha himself who initiates them.

The passage that follows, within the section on the conditions for miscellaneous wholesome deeds, states: "Also, may all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of future ages... and so forth; this is precisely that text.
6. Reconciling contradictions between the Sūtras and the Śāstras by providing extensive questions and answers to dispel doubts.
Within this section, there are six parts: first, presenting the interpretations of various Dharma masters regarding the meaning of the nine grades;

second, refuting them through logical reasoning; third, reiterating the nine grades to counter-argue and refute [the previous positions]; fourth, citing textual evidence to prove definitively that these refer to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and not to noble ones (*ārya*); fifth, harmonizing the intent of the "specific time" (*kāla-viśeṣa*) teaching; and sixth, harmonizing the meaning of the non-arising of the seeds of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Regarding the initial statement that "the various masters explain [this]," it first cites the three classes of practitioners,
beginning with the "superior-superior" (shang-shang). These refer to Bodhisattvas from the fourth stage up to the seventh stage.
How is this known? Because upon reaching that stage, one immediately attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
Those of superior-middle capacity are bodhisattvas from the first through the fourth bhūmis.
How is this known?
Because by reaching that [stage], one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) after the passing of a small kalpa.
"Above and below" refers to Bodhisattvas from the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) up to the first bhūmi.
How is this known?
Because it is stated that one enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) only after three intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*) have passed since reaching that [state].
These three types of persons are all noble beings (*ārya*) of the Mahāyāna who have attained the state of birth.
Next, regarding the three individuals of the middle grade,
various masters say:
"The upper and middle [grades] are persons who have attained the three fruits."
How is this known?
Because by reaching that stage, one immediately attains arhatship.
The "middling-of-the-middling" refers to the inner ordinary person (antarapudgala).
How is this known?
It is because they have attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
Those of middling and inferior capacity are worldly virtuous ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who, weary of suffering, seek rebirth.
How is this known?
Because by reaching that [state], one attains the fruit of Arhatship after the passing of one small kalpa.
These three grades consist exclusively of noble ones of the Hīnayāna.

Regarding the three grades of the lower class, these are ordinary beings who have newly begun their study of the Mahāyāna; they are divided into three categories according to the lightness or gravity of their transgressions, yet they share a single rank.
It should be understood that this does not necessarily apply to those who seek rebirth through the power of their vows alone.
Second, as for refuting [the opponent's position] by means of reasoning:
regarding the aforementioned statement that bodhisattvas from the first stage up to the seventh stage are [as described],
it is as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"From the first stage up to the seventh stage, these are the Dharma-nature birth-body and the transformation birth-body.
Such beings have never experienced the suffering of分段 (segmented) death."

Regarding their efficacy, they have already passed through two great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, simultaneously cultivating both merit and wisdom, as well as the two types of emptiness—of persons and phenomena.
Both are inconceivable, with supernatural powers that are sovereign and transformations that know no limit.
Dwelling in the land of retribution, you constantly hear the Dharma being preached by the Buddha of retribution.

Your compassionate transformation pervades the ten directions in an instant; what more is there to worry about that you would rely on Vaidehī to entreat the Buddha for her sake, seeking rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss?
Based on this textual evidence, how could the explanations of the various masters not be erroneous?
This concludes the response to the preceding two points.
Regarding "above and below":
The previous statement that [this applies] from the spiritual lineage (gotra) up to the first stage (bhūmi) is not necessarily so.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"These bodhisattvas are called 'non-retrogressive'."
"Though dwelling within birth and death, one is not defiled by birth and death.
It is like a goose or a duck in water; the water cannot wet them.
As it is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"In this stage, the bodhisattva does not regress because they are protected by two kinds of true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
What are these two?
The first is the Buddhas of the ten directions."

Second, the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions constantly apply their three karmas externally to all wholesome dharmas without any regression or loss; therefore, this is called the stage of non-retrogression.
"These bodhisattvas are likewise able to manifest the eightfold path to enlightenment and transform sentient beings.
As for their meritorious practices, they have already passed through one great asaṃkhyeya kalpa, cultivating both merit and wisdom in equal measure."
Since such supreme virtues already exist, what further matter is there to worry about that one must rely upon Vaidehī’s request to seek birth [in the Pure Land]?
This is evidenced by this very text.
Therefore, we know that the judgments of the various masters have, in fact, resulted in error.
This concludes the critique of the senior practitioners.
Next, regarding the critique of the three types of intermediate practitioners,
the various masters say:
Regarding those who attain the three fruits among the middle and upper grades:
such individuals shall forever sever the three miserable realms and will not be reborn in the four destinies.
Although they may commit sinful karma in the present life, they will certainly not incur retribution in the future.
As the Buddha has said:
"These four types of fruit-attainers sit upon the same bed of liberation as I.
Since they already possess such power and merit, why should they have further cause for anxiety that they must rely on Vaidehī’s request to seek a path to rebirth?

However, because the great compassion of all Buddhas is directed toward those who suffer, their hearts are especially moved by sentient beings who are constantly submerged [in saṃsāra]; for this reason, they exhort them to take refuge in the Pure Land.
It is just as when a person is drowning, one must urgently provide rescue specifically for them.
As for those already on the shore, what need is there for them to cross?
Using this text as evidence, we know that the judgments of the various masters are erroneous in the same manner as before;
this can be understood from what follows.
Third, regarding the reiteration of the nine grades to refute [the opposing view]:
various masters state that those who attain the highest grade of the highest birth are bodhisattvas from the fourth bhūmi up to the seventh bhūmi.
For what reason does the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* state:
"Three kinds of sentient beings shall attain rebirth.
What are the three?":
First, those who are able to maintain the precepts and cultivate loving-kindness;
second, those who are unable to maintain the precepts and cultivate loving-kindness, but are able to read and recite the Mahāyāna;
third, those who are unable to maintain the precepts or read the scriptures, but are only able to mindfully recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.
These three individuals each applied themselves with single-minded diligence and focused intent to their respective tasks.
They continued without interruption for one day and one night, and even up to seven days and seven nights.
Each shall turn back their karmic actions and pray for rebirth there.

Each and every kind of precious object consisted of five hundred carriages.

With hundreds of thousands of millions of people offering incense, flowers, and music, they praised him and surrounded him as he was escorted toward the assembly of the Buddha to be offered to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Upon seeing this, Devadatta’s envy intensified further, and he immediately went to Śāriputra to request instruction in the supernormal power of bodily mastery.
The Venerable One said to him:
"Virtuous one, you should first practice the four foundations of mindfulness; there is no need to study the supernormal power of bodily mastery."

Since his request was not granted, he went further to seek instruction from other venerable ones; eventually, among all five hundred disciples, there was no one who would teach him, and they all sent him away to study the four foundations of mindfulness.
Having no other choice, he then went to Ānanda to study.
He said to Ānanda, "You are my younger brother;
I wish to learn the Abhidharma, so please instruct me step by step in its entirety."

However, although Ānanda had attained the first fruit of the path, he had not yet realized the knowledge of others' minds; thus, he did not know that his elder brother’s secret studies were so thorough that he intended to harbor evil designs toward the Buddha.
Ānanda then immediately led him to a quiet place and instructed him step by step.

He first taught him to sit upright in the full lotus posture and direct the mind to lift the body, imagining it moving; then to imagine it rising one *fen*, one *cun*, one *chi*, and one *zhang* above the ground; continuing until he imagines the dwelling as empty and unobstructed, passing straight up into the midst of space; finally, withdrawing the mind back down to the original seat.

Next, one shall lift the mind with the body; at first, rising from the ground by a fraction of an inch or a finger-breadth, it is done according to the previous method. By lifting the mind with the body and the body with the mind, once the mind has ascended to the upper sky, one then draws it back down to the original seat.
Next, visualize the body and mind rising together; as before, they move in unison through increments of one part or one inch, repeating the cycle.
Next, visualize the body and mind entering into all material, obstructive forms, while maintaining the perception that they are non-obstructive.
Next, visualize all mountains, rivers, the great earth, and so forth, entering into one's own body; like space, they are unimpeded, and no physical forms are seen.

Next, visualize one’s own body as either vast, filling the entirety of space, sitting or lying down with ease—whether sitting or reclining—one can grasp and move the sun and moon with one's hands; or, manifesting a minute body, enter into a mote of dust. In all these instances, cultivate the perception of total non-obstruction.

After Ānanda had thus instructed him in this sequence, Devadatta, having received the Dharma, went separately to a quiet place. For seven days and seven nights, he focused his mind with single-minded concentration and immediately attained supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), achieving mastery in all things.
Having attained these supernatural powers, he immediately went before the prince’s palace and manifested great miraculous transformations in mid-air.

Fire issued from his upper body while water issued from his lower body; at times water issued from his left side and fire from his right, or he manifested a massive body or a minute body. He sat or lay within the air, moving with complete mastery and ease according to his will.
Having seen this, the Prince asked his attendants,
"Who is this person?
His attendants replied to the Prince:
"This is the Venerable Deva.
Upon hearing this, the Prince was filled with great joy; he immediately raised his hand and called out, "Venerable One, why do you not come down?"
When Deva saw that he had been summoned, he immediately transformed himself into an infant and went straight onto the Prince’s lap.
The Prince took him up, kissed his mouth, and played with him; he then spat into the infant’s mouth, and the infant swallowed it.
In an instant, he returned to his original form.
Having witnessed Deva’s various miraculous transformations, the Prince’s reverence increased all the more.
Once he perceived the Prince’s deep respect, Deva immediately recounted the circumstances of his father the King’s offerings.
There were five hundred different varieties of colors, which were loaded onto chariots and taken to the Buddha’s location to be offered to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
Upon hearing this, the Prince immediately said to the Venerable One:

"I, your disciple, am also able to prepare five hundred chariots of each of these various colors to offer to you, Venerable One, and to bestow upon the assembly of monks; why should I not do as they have?"
Devadatta said,
"Prince, this intention of yours is most excellent.
From that time forward, he received great offerings, and his mind became increasingly arrogant.
It is just as when one strikes an evil dog on the nose with a stick; the dog’s wickedness only increases further. This case is exactly like that:
the Prince now uses the stick of gain and offerings to strike the dog’s nose of Devadatta’s greedy mind, causing his wickedness to become even more rampant.
Therefore, I shall split the Sangha and alter the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya so that their precepts differ.

When the Buddha universally preaches the Dharma for the great assembly of both ordinary beings and sages, I will come into that gathering and request from the Buddha that his disciples, as well as all the Dharma treasuries, be entirely entrusted to me.
"The World-Honored One is now advanced in years; he should retire to a quiet place to nourish himself.
When the entire assembly heard these words from Deva, they stared at one another in astonishment, filled with great wonder and alarm.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Deva before the great assembly, saying:
"Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others are indeed great leaders of the Dharma; I would not even entrust the Buddha-dharma to them."
"How much more so for you, a foolish man who eats spittle!
When Deva heard the Buddha disparage him before the assembly in this way, it was as if a poisoned arrow had entered his heart, causing him to give rise once more to a state of delirious madness.
On account of this, they went together to where the Prince was and discussed their evil scheme.
When the Prince saw the Venerable One, he received him with a respectful mind and asked:
"Venerable One, the color of your face today is haggard and unlike that of former days."
Devadatta replied,
"I am now so emaciated precisely because of the Prince.
The Prince asked with respect:
"What is your intention toward me,
Venerable Sir? Deva replied,
"Does the Prince not know?"
"The World-Honored One is aged and no longer capable of his duties; he should be relieved of them, so that I may become a Buddha myself.
Our father the King is also aged and may likewise be relieved of his duties, so that the Crown Prince may sit upon the throne of sovereignty."
"Is it not a joy that a new king and a new Buddha are ruling and transforming the world?
Upon hearing this, the Prince became extremely enraged and said, "Do not speak such words!
He further said:
"Prince, do not be angry.
Your father, the King, has shown you no kindness or virtue whatsoever.

When he first desired for you to be born, the King immediately sent your mother up onto a hundred-foot tower to give birth beneath the skylight, intending for you to fall to the ground and die. It was solely due to the power of your merit that your life-force was not severed, though your little finger was damaged."
"If you do not believe me, look at your own little finger; this shall serve as proof.
Having heard these words, the Prince examined them once more and asked with renewed earnestness:
"Is it truly so?"
Devadatta replied, "If this were not true, I would have come here merely to speak empty words.
Having said these words, he then placed his trust in Devadatta’s evil scheme; thus it is said that he followed the teachings of the evil friend Devadatta.
3. From the passage beginning with "Having seized his father the king" down to "not one was able to go," the text clearly elucidates that the father-king was imprisoned by his son.

This demonstrates how Ajātaśatru, adopting the evil stratagem of Devadatta, abruptly abandoned the affection between father and son; he not only forfeited the debt of infinite gratitude, but the echoes of his rebellion filled the roads.
Suddenly covering the King’s body, he said, "Seize! Having captured him and not letting him go, he said, "Hold! Thus it is called "seizing and holding.
To speak of him as "Father" specifically reveals the ultimate limit of intimacy.
"King" signifies his rank;
"Bimbisāra" signifies his name.
As for the statement that he was confined within seven layers of inner chambers:
Since the purpose is weighty, the matter is likewise no trivial one.
It is not possible to prohibit it lightly among the people, leaving it entirely without protection.
However, as for the King’s palace quarters, by their very nature they are inaccessible to outsiders; only the ministers have long served there.
If strict regulations were not established, there would be fear of illicit relations between sentient beings;
therefore, they were made to sever all external ties and were confined within seven layers of enclosure.
Fourth, from the passage beginning with "the Great Lady of the State" down to "above Mi, the King," this clearly explains how the lady secretly served food to the King.
The term "State Great Lady" (Guo Dafuren) clarifies her supreme status.
The term "Lady" (Furen) designates her rank.
The term "Vaidehī" reveals her personal name.
Regarding the phrase "respectfully addressing the Great King":
this clarifies that when the lady saw the King’s body imprisoned and the gates so strictly guarded that no news could pass through, she feared for the King’s very life.

Thereupon, he immediately bathed in scented water to purify his body; he then took ghee and honey and first smeared them upon his body, after which he took parched grain and placed it atop the ghee and honey.
She immediately put on clean garments over her outer clothes and then began to don her necklaces, dressing according to her usual custom so as not to arouse suspicion among outsiders.
She then took one end of a necklace and plugged its hole with wax; at the other end, she filled the hole with grape juice and sealed it once it was full.
However, all her ornaments were likewise like this.
Once she had finished adorning herself, she entered the palace at a leisurely pace to meet with the king.
He asked:
"The ministers, having received the royal decree, have not permitted me to see the King.
I do not understand why the lady’s household has not been restricted and allowed me entry; what is the intention behind this?"
He replied:
"The ministers are of different bodies and are outsiders; fearing that there might be illicit intimacy between them, I have imposed these strict prohibitions.
Furthermore, as for the lady, she is a woman by body and has no ulterior motives in her heart."

Due to the heavy karmic affinity from our past lives, we have been husband and wife for a long time; though our bodies are distinct, our hearts are one, such that people have no cause for external suspicion.
For this reason, I was able to enter and meet with the King.

5. From the passage "At that time, the Great King ate the parched grain" down to "having bestowed upon me the eight precepts," this clearly elucidates how the Father King, due to his observance of the prohibitions, requested the Dharma.
This clarifies that once the Queen saw the King, she immediately scraped the *sū* (clarified butter) and parched grain from her own body, formed them into a ball, and presented it to the King.
The king obtained it and ate immediately.
Having finished eating the parched grain,
he had pure water fetched from within the palace by his consort to rinse his mouth.
Having completed the purification of the mouth, one must not spend time in vain; for the mind has no place to rest.
Therefore, with reverent palms joined, turn the face toward Gṛdhrakūṭa and pay homage to the Tathāgata, entreating him for his protective empowerment.
This clarifies the respect shown through bodily action (*kāyakarman*), which also extends to include mental action (*manaskarman*).
The passage beginning with "Having spoken these words" correctly clarifies the request made through verbal action (*vākkarman*), which likewise extends to include mental action.
Regarding the statement that Mahāmaudgalyāyana was my close friend, there are two meanings to it.

While Maudgalyāyana was in secular life, he was the king’s personal relative; once he had left the household life, he became my teacher. Thus, his coming and going within the palace gates was entirely without hindrance.
However, while he was a layman he was a kinsman, and having left the household life he is called a friend; thus he is termed a "kinsman-friend.

As for the words, "I pray that you will arouse compassion and grant me the eight precepts," this clarifies that the King, his father, possesses a profound depth of devotion to the Dharma and values others more than himself.
If one has not encountered profound adversity, it is no great difficulty to invite the Buddha and the Sangha;
but now that I am imprisoned, there is no way to fulfill such a request.
Therefore, I shall simply ask Maudgalyāyana to receive the Eight Precepts on my behalf.
Question:
"The Father King paid homage from afar, first prostrating before the World-Honored One.
When he received the precepts, he immediately invited Maudgalyāyana."
"What is the meaning of this?
He replied, "Among all beings, from the ordinary to the sage, none are more supreme than the Buddha; therefore, having inclined my heart and made my vow, I first pay homage to the Great Teacher."
The precepts are a minor matter; therefore, he requested only Maudgalyāyana to come and confer them.

However, the King’s intention was that it would suffice to ensure the attainment of the precepts, as this would fulfill the purpose; why then trouble the World-Honored One with such a circuitous journey?
He asked, "The precepts of the Tathāgata are indeed immeasurable.
Why did my father the King request only the eight precepts and not the others?"
He replied:
"The other precepts are somewhat lax and their duration is long; I fear that in the interim one might lose mindfulness and wander through birth and death.
As for these eight precepts, as explained in other Buddhist sūtras, they are the monastic precepts observed by laypeople."
This precept involves maintaining the mind with extreme subtlety and intensity. Why is this so?
Because the duration is quite brief, limited to only one day and night, after which it is relinquished once the ritual procedure is completed.
How is it known that the mental application of this precept is subtle?
It is fully revealed in the text of the precepts,
which states:
"O Son of the Buddha, from this morning until tomorrow morning, for one day and one night, can you maintain the precept of not killing, as all Buddhas do?
He replied:
"I can maintain it."
The second [text] further states:

"O Son of the Buddha, from this morning until tomorrow morning, for one day and one night, as the Buddhas do not steal, do not engage in sexual misconduct, do not speak falsely, do not drink alcohol, do not apply ointments or powders to the body, do not perform or attend dances, songs, or theatrical performances, and do not sit upon high or wide beds—these eight items above are precepts (*śīla*), not fasts (*upavāsa*)."
"One must not eat past midday; this one item is a fast (upavāsa), not a precept (śīla).
All these various precepts take all the Buddhas as witnesses. Why is this?"
Only among Buddhas and Buddhas are both the afflictions and their residual habits completely exhausted.
Apart from the Buddhas, the residual habits of evil and so forth still remain.
For this reason, they are not cited as proof.
Therefore, one should know that the application of mind and the undertaking of practice regarding this precept are extremely subtle and urgent.
Furthermore, the Buddha has taught that this precept possesses eight kinds of superior qualities.
If a person maintains it fully for even one day and one night without transgression, the merit obtained surpasses the realms of humans, devas, and the two vehicles.
As explained at length in the sutra, because there was such benefit, it caused the father-king to receive it day by day.

Sixth, from the time Mahāmaudgalyāyana descended until he had finished preaching the Dharma for the king, it is clarified that the father-king, through his invitation, was able to receive the noble Dharma.

This man of clear vision, having attained the knowledge of others' minds, knew from afar his father the king's intention; he immediately manifested supernatural powers and reached the king's presence in the time it takes to snap one's fingers.
Furthermore, fearing that people might not recognize the characteristics of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), he employs the swift falcon as a metaphor.

However, as for Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal power, in the space of a single thought-moment he circumambulates the four continents a hundred thousand times; how could this possibly be compared to a falcon?
There are many such comparisons that cannot be cited in full, as explained in detail in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*.
Regarding the statement that he thus bestowed the eight precepts upon the king every day:
This clarifies that the King, his father, extended his life so that Maudgalyāyana could come repeatedly to receive the precepts.
He asked:
"If these Eight Precepts are said to be superior, then receiving them once would suffice."
"Why must one receive it day after day?

He replied: "Mountains do not weary of being high; the ocean does not weary of being deep; a blade does not weary of being sharp; the sun does not weary of its brightness; people do not weary of goodness; sin does not weary of being eliminated; the worthy do not weary of virtue; and the Buddha does not weary of his holiness."
However, as for the King’s intention, now that he has been imprisoned, he no longer receives permission to move about.
In every thought-moment, he fears being summoned for execution.
For this reason, day and night he directs his whole heart toward relying upon the eight precepts, hoping to accumulate merit and increase his virtue to provide support for his future karma.
Regarding the statement that the World-Honored One also dispatched Pūrṇa to preach the Dharma to the king:

this clarifies that the World-Honored One’s compassionate intent was profound, as he took pity on the king’s person having suddenly encountered the hardship of imprisonment and feared he might fall into distress and exhaustion.
However, Pūrṇa is the foremost among the noble disciples in expounding the Dharma; he is skilled in employing expedient means to awaken the minds of others.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has dispatched him to preach the Dharma for the king, so as to eliminate his sorrow and distress.

7. From the passage beginning with "At such a time" down to "the complexion became serene," it is clearly explained that the Father King, having heard the Dharma while eating, did not die for many days.
This passage clearly explains that the lady served food for a long time to alleviate their hunger and thirst.
Furthermore, the two sages used the internal sustenance of the Dharma of the precepts to skillfully open the King’s mind.
Food can prolong life, while the Dharma of the precepts nourishes the spirit; by eliminating suffering and extinguishing grief, it causes the countenance to become harmonious and joyful.
Although there have been seven different sections above, the detailed explanation regarding the circumstances of forbidding [the father] is now complete.
Third, within the section concerning the circumstances of forbidding [the mother], there are eight parts.
First, from the passage beginning with "At that time, Ajātaśatru" down to "is she still living? correctly clarifies the inquiry regarding news of his father.

This clarifies that since King Ajātaśatru had confined his father for so many days, all human contact was completely severed and even water and food were not permitted; with more than two weeks having passed, the father’s life should have come to an end.
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to the palace gate and asked the gatekeeper:
"Does my father, the King, still live?
He asked thus:
"If a person eats a single meal and their life is limited to seven days, they will die;
since my father the King has already passed three weeks, his life must have ended without a doubt.
Why did King Ajātaśatru not simply ask [the physician] directly?"
"Gatekeeper, has our father, the King, now truly passed away?
Why do you ask with such doubt as if he were still alive? What is your intention?
He replied:
"This was King Ajātaśatru’s secret inquiry.
However, as the sovereign of ten thousand foundations, his every movement must not be left to mere convenience.
Since the Father King is of such heavenly nature and so deeply affectionate, it was impossible for him to speak of death."
I feared that failing to act at that time would lead to reproach and censure.
Therefore, I marked my own death with my inner mind while asking about those who remained, desiring thereby to silence the long-standing sound of such evil and rebellious conduct.
2. From the point where the gatekeeper says, "At that time," down to "cannot be restrained," this precisely clarifies how the gatekeeper answered the matter in full.
This explains that while Ajātaśatru previously asked whether his father the king was present, it is now the turn of the gatekeeper to provide the formal reply.
He addressed the Great King, saying, "From the Chief Queen of the kingdom downward, the Lady Zhengming has secretly offered this food to Your Majesty.
Once the King has partaken of this food, it shall prolong his life."
Although many days have passed, the father’s life remains;
this is due to the lady’s intention and is not the fault of the family.
He asked:
"The lady served the food while her body was smeared with flour and she was closely covered from head to toe as she entered and exited; no one could see her.
For what reason, then, do you display the matter of the lady serving food so conspicuously at the gate?"
He replied, "All private secrets cannot be maintained for long; even if hidden with skillful care, the matter will eventually be revealed.
Since my father the King has confined me within the palace, the Queen visits daily. If I do not secretly carry this flour-food, there is no way for the King’s life to be sustained."
Now, as for what is called "secret," it was intended to convey the lady's intentions to the family;
the lady believed her words were secret and unknown to outsiders, yet the entire family had already perceived them.
"Now that the matter has reached its limit, there is no way to conceal it; therefore, I have related everything in detail to Your Majesty.

From the mention of the śramaṇa Maudgalyāyana onwards, this clearly explains how the two sages travel through the air, not by way of gates or paths, coming and going every day to preach the Dharma for the king.
"Your Majesty should know that when the lady presented the food, she did not first receive Your Majesty’s command; therefore, she did not dare to offer any restrictions.
Furthermore, as these two sages traveled through the air, this was likewise beyond the scope of the gate regulations."
Third, from the passage where Ajātaśatru hears these words downward, until the point where he intends to harm his mother, this clearly elucidates King Ajātaśatru’s wrath.
This demonstrates that once King Ajātaśatru had heard the family’s explanation, he immediately conceived evil anger toward the Queen and uttered harsh words.
Furthermore, one may commit the three types of perversions (ānantarya) and the three types of evil through the three karmas.
To revile one's parents as thieves is called the perversion of verbal karma;
to revile a śramaṇa is called the evil of verbal karma.
To seize a sword and kill one’s mother is called an *ānantarya* (immediate) transgression of bodily action (*kāyakarma*).
Since that which is performed by body and speech has the mind as its sovereign, this is also called an *ānantarya* transgression of mental action (*manaskarma*).
Furthermore, the preliminary preparation (*prayoga*) constitutes the evil, while the subsequent actual deed (*maula-karman*) constitutes the transgression.
From the words "My mother is a thief" onwards, the text clearly demonstrates the utterance of evil speech.
How does he revile his mother as a thief?
She is a companion of thieves.
However, King Ajātaśatru’s original intent was to harbor resentment toward his father, regretting that he had not died sooner.
His mother then secretly provided him with food so that he would not die;
for this reason, she spoke these words of reproach:
"My mother is a thief; she is an accomplice of thieves.

Regarding the passage beginning with "The śramaṇas are evil people," this clarifies that when Ajātaśatru was about to offer food to his mother, he further heard that the śramaṇas were coming and going with the king, which caused him to give rise once more to a mind of hatred.
Therefore it is said: "By what incantation or spell can this evil king be kept from dying for so many days?
The passage beginning with "As soon as he spoke, he seized a sharp sword" clarifies that the worldly king’s rage was so intense that it even turned against his own mother.
How painful it was! Grasping his head as he brandished a sword, his life hung by a mere thread.
His compassionate mother joined her palms, bent her body, and lowered her head to reach for her son’s hand.
At that time, the lady’s hot sweat flowed all over her body and her mind became faint and bewildered.
Alas, how tragic!
In a moment of dazed confusion, she encountered this bitter suffering.

4. From the time when a minister named Candraprabha descended from above and withdrew by retreating backward, it clearly illustrates how the two ministers earnestly admonished [the king], yet he would not listen.

This clarifies that these two ministers are the pillars of the state and the fundamental framework for establishing governance; it is hoped they will bring renown to the myriad nations and initiate the practice of virtue throughout the eight directions.
Suddenly, he saw King Ajātaśatru rise up in rebellion, grasping a sword and intending to kill his mother.
Unable to bear witnessing such an evil deed, he then, together with Jīvaka, ventured to remonstrate against the king’s countenance.
Regarding the phrase "at that time," it refers to the period when King Ajātaśatru was about to kill his mother.
Regarding the mention of "a great minister," this indicates his official rank.
Regarding the mention of "Moonlight," this indicates his personal name.
To say he was "intelligent and possessed of great wisdom" is to manifest his virtue.
As for the mention of Jīvaka, Jīvaka was also the son of the King, the father; he was the child of Queen Nāla.
Suddenly seeing his elder brother plotting rebellion against their mother, he and Candraprabha together offered counsel.
He said that regarding the act of prostrating before a king: whenever one wishes to consult or advise a superior, it is essential to perform a formal salutation to manifest one's physical respect.

Now these two ministers are likewise: first they established physical reverence to awaken and move the King’s mind, and only after folding their hands and bowing did they set forth their original intent.

Furthermore, when they addressed the Great King as "O Great King," this Moonlight (Candraprabha) was precisely about to present his words, hoping that King Śreṇika would open his heart to listen and receive them.
For this reason, one must first address him, saying:
"Your servant has heard what is taught in the *Veda* scriptures; this clarifies the extensive citation of ancient and modern books and histories, as well as the records of successive emperors."
The ancients said: "Speech that does not relate to the classics is a source of shame for the gentleman.
Since the matter of this admonition is no trivial one, how could it be based on empty words or reckless assertions?
By stating that it has been so since the beginning of the kalpa, he clarifies its timing.
The phrase "there are various evil kings" clarifies that this is a general designation for those who are impolite, violent, and rebellious.
The phrase "because they covet the position of the state" clarifies that it is not their own intention that they covet, but rather that they seize the seat of their father.

Regarding the statement "he killed his father," this clarifies that since one has given rise to such evil toward one's father, it is not permissible to remain [in that state] for long; therefore, it was necessary to take his life.
Regarding the statement "eighteen thousand," this clarifies that the King’s current killing of his father is identical to those [previous instances].

To say that one has never heard of an unrighteous person who harmed his mother is to claim that, from antiquity to the present, while historical records abound with accounts of those who harmed their fathers to seize the throne, there is no record whatsoever of anyone killing their mother out of greed for the kingdom.

If we discuss the period since the beginning of the kalpa, wicked kings were greedy for their kingdoms and killed only their fathers while sparing their compassionate mothers; this would be citing the past to contrast with the present.
Your Majesty now, out of greed for the kingdom, has killed your father; as for the father, he held a position that could be coveted, so one might argue his case is similar to those of antiquity.
But as for the mother, she had no position to seek; you have nonetheless committed a rebellious act of harm against her. For this reason, the present differs from the past.
To say that the King has now killed his mother for this reason is to defile the Kṣatriya caste.
As for the Kṣatriyas, they are the highest origin of the four castes and the lineage of kings; transmitted from generation to generation, how could they be equated with commoners?

When I say that I cannot bear to hear it, it is because I see the King giving rise to evil, which brings disgrace and humiliation upon his kinsmen and causes an evil reputation to spread; for my own character and aspirations, there would be no ground left for shame or modesty.
To speak of this *caṇḍāla* is to refer to the lowest dregs of the four castes.
By nature he harbors a cruel and malevolent heart and is unacquainted with benevolence and righteousness; though he wears human skin, his conduct is identical to that of birds and beasts.

The King resides within the highest lineage and is the sovereign presiding over the foundation of ten thousand states; yet now that he has given rise to evil and abandoned his benevolence, how does he differ from those of the lowest stratum?
As for the statement that it is improper for him to remain here, there are two meanings:
first, the King now commits evil and no longer observes the rites of propriety; how could the capital, the land of the Central Kingdom, allow a *caṇḍāla* to be its ruler?
This is precisely the intention behind banishing him from the palace city.

Second, although the king remains within the kingdom, he harms my kinsmen; it would be better to exile him far away to a remote region where he will never again be heard of, which is why it was said that he should not remain here.

Regarding the statement that after the two ministers had spoken these words, this clarifies that the two ministers offered direct admonition with extremely blunt language, extensively citing examples from antiquity and the present in hopes of opening the King’s mind to enlightenment.
Regarding the statement "pressing his hand upon his sword," the subject was merely pressing the sword held in his own hand.
He asked:

"Your remonstrance was coarse and harsh, and you did not shrink from offending the sovereign's countenance. Since the righteousness between ruler and minister has thus been violated, why did you not simply turn your body and depart directly, instead of saying that you withdrew by retreating?"
He replied:

"Although my coarse words were contrary to the King's wishes, I hoped they would cause him to cease his intent to harm my mother. Furthermore, fearing that the poison of his anger had not yet been removed and that he might draw his sword to endanger me, I gripped my blade for self-protection and withdrew by retreating."
5. From the passage beginning with "At that time, Ajātaśatru was struck with terror" down to "Do you not act for my sake? it precisely clarifies that King Ajātaśatru gave rise to fear.

This explains that once Ajātaśatru saw the two ministers’ admonitions were harsh and cutting, and further observed them sheathing their swords and departing, he feared they would turn against him and go over to his father, the King, thereby devising further treacherous schemes.
Consequently, my feelings were unsettled, and thus I was called "terrified.
Since he had already abandoned me, I did not know who he might be.
With doubts unresolved in my mind, I immediately questioned him with my own mouth to ascertain the truth.
Therefore it is said, "Jīvaka, you have not done this for me.
Jīvaka was the younger brother of the king.
An ancient said:
When a family faces calamity, no one but a kinsman will come to its rescue.
Since you are my younger brother, how could you be like Candraprabha?
Sixth, from the passage where Jīvaka addresses [the King] down to "be careful not to harm your mother," it clarifies the earnest remonstrance of the two ministers.
This clarifies that Jīvaka answered the Great King truthfully: "If you wish to have us as your ministers, I pray that you do not harm our mother.
This concludes the direct admonition.

Seventh, from the passage where the King hears these words down to the point where he desists from harming the mother, it correctly clarifies how King Ajātaśatru accepted the admonition and spared the mother's remaining life.

This clarifies that once King Śreṇiya had received Jīvaka’s admonition, remorse arose within his heart; feeling shame for what he had previously done, he immediately sought mercy from the two ministers and begged for his life.
Consequently, he released his mother, freeing her from the peril of death.
The sword in his hand returned to its original sheath.

Eighth, from the passage "the palace eunuch descended according to the imperial decree" down to "not allowing him to emerge again," it clarifies that the former king’s lingering resentment prohibited the mother from leaving.
This clarifies that although King Śreṇiya accepted his minister’s admonition and released his mother, he still harbored residual anger and would not allow her to remain outside.
He commanded his inner officials to confine her within the deep palace and strictly forbid her from coming out to meet her father, the king.
Although there have been eight distinct points above,
this concludes the detailed explanation of the causes regarding the prohibition against mothers.
Fourth, within the context of the causes for revulsion toward suffering, there are four points.
First: From the time Vaidehī descended [the stairs] until she became emaciated, this section clearly explains that the Queen was imprisoned for her son’s sake.

This clarifies that although the Queen strove to escape her mortal peril, she was instead confined further within the inner palace; guarded by the strictest guards, there was no way for her to emerge.
Only by constantly harboring grief did she naturally become emaciated.
She lamented, saying: "Alas!
How bitter is my fate this day; having encountered King Ajātaśatru’s summons, I am bound between sharp blades and cast into the hardship of the deep palace."
Question:
"Since the lady has managed to escape death and enter the palace, she ought to feel joy; for what reason, instead, does she feel such sorrow and anxiety? Answer:
"There are three points of distinction here.

First, since the lady herself has been confined, no one else can enter to provide food for the King; moreover, hearing that I am in distress, the King’s sorrow and anxiety will only increase further."
Now that they have no food and are further burdened by grief, the King’s life will surely not last much longer.
As for the Second Noble Lady, having been imprisoned in such hardship, when will she ever again behold the face of the Tathāgata and his disciples?

The three consorts, having been commanded to observe strict seclusion within the inner palace, were guarded by eunuchs so that not even a drop of water could leak out; from dawn until dusk, they could think of nothing but the path to death.
With these three circumstances pressing upon their bodies and minds, it is no wonder they have become so withered and haggard.

2. From the moment she descended from afar toward Vulture Peak until the point before she had even raised her head, it was precisely during this interval that the Lady Zhengming, having invited the Buddha due to her observance of the precepts, had something she wished to state.
This clarifies that since the Lady was imprisoned, she had no means of reaching the Buddha’s presence in person.

She could only turn her heart single-mindedly toward Gṛdhrakūṭa, prostrating from afar to the World-Honored One, and pray with compassion that the Buddha would take note of her disciple’s state of sorrow and anxiety.
Regarding the passage beginning with "When the Tathāgata was in the past," there are two meanings.

First, it clarifies that before the father-king was placed under restraint, either the king and I personally went to the Buddha’s side, or the Tathāgata and his disciples personally accepted the king’s invitation.
However, since both my person and that of the King are imprisoned, our means of communication have been severed and our mutual feelings estranged.
Second, ever since the Father King has been in confinement, the World-Honored One has frequently sent Ānanda to come and console me.
What is meant by "offering consolation"?
Because the father-king was seen to be imprisoned, the Buddha feared that the Queen would suffer from grief and distress; for this reason, he sent [the messenger] to offer consolation.
As for the statement, "The World-Honored One is majestic and grave, making it impossible to have an audience," it means:

This clarifies that the lady, inwardly humble and self-effacing, places her respect in the disciples of the Buddha; for her defiled female body possesses meager causes of merit, and the Buddha’s virtue and majesty are so sublime that she has no means to encounter him lightly; she prays that Maudgalyāyana and others be sent to meet her.
Question:
"The Tathāgata is the master of emanations and should not fail to act at the appropriate time.
Why did he not make three successive requests himself, but instead summon Maudgalyāyana and the others? What was his intention?"
He replied, “The Buddha’s virtue is most majestic and solemn; I did not dare to request an audience on such a minor matter.
However, seeing Ānanda, I wished to entrust him with a message to go and inform the World-Honored One.”
"The Buddha, knowing my intention, again had Ānanda convey the Buddha’s words and give me instruction; for this reason, I wish to see Ānanda.
By saying these words, he concluded his previous explanation of the matter.

Regarding the phrase "weeping with tears falling like rain," this clarifies that the lady, realizing her own transgressions were grave, entreated the Buddha to extend his compassion; her reverence was so profound that sorrowful tears filled her eyes.
It is merely because of my yearning for the sacred countenance that I have further added this prostration from afar, bowing my head to the ground and remaining there for a moment without rising.

Third, from the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One descended" down to "the heavenly flowers were taken to make offerings," it clearly illustrates that the World-Honored One came in person to accept the invitation.
This clarifies that although the World-Honored One was at Gṛdhrakūṭa, he already knew the thoughts in the queen’s mind.
As for the statement that he commanded Mahāmaudgalyāyana and others to come through the air, this clarifies that he responded to the queen’s invitation.
As for the statement that the Buddha passed away on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, this clarifies that the restrictions within the palace of the Queen were extremely strict.
It was feared that if the Buddha were to manifest his presence and come there, King Ajātaśatru might hear of it and create further obstacles.
For these reasons, it was necessary for him to vanish from here and appear there.
As for the statement that Vaidehī raised her head after prostrating, this clarifies the moment when the lady paid her respects.
Regarding the phrase "seeing the World-Honored Buddha," this clarifies that the World-Honored One has already emerged from his palace, causing the lady to raise her head and see him immediately.
Regarding the name "Śākyamuni Buddha," this distinguishes him from other Buddhas.

However, while the names of all Buddhas are common [to one another], their physical characteristics do not differ; it is for this reason that Śākyamuni is now specifically identified to eliminate any doubt.
The statement that "his body is purple-gold in color" serves to definitively establish his specific appearance.
The phrase "seated upon flowers of a hundred jewels" distinguishes this seat from all others.
The statement that "Maudgalyāyana attended on the left," and so forth, clarifies that there were no other assemblies present, but only these two groups of monks.

Regarding the mention of Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors: this clarifies that the assembly of celestial kings and others, seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, appearing and disappearing within the royal palace, will surely proclaim his marvelous and extraordinary teachings.
We gods and humans, because of Vaidehī, have obtained the benefit of hearing what we had never heard before.
Each mounting our original resolve, we dwell together throughout the air; with divine ears, we hear from afar and partake of the offerings of raining flowers.
Furthermore, that which is called "Śakra" is the Lord of Devas (Indra).
That which is called "Brahmā" refers to the Brahmā Kings and others of the Form Realm.
That which is called "World-Protector" refers to the Four Heavenly Kings.
Regarding the phrase "the various devas," this refers to the assemblies of devas in the realms of form and desire.
Having seen the Heavenly King approach the Buddha, those various deva assemblies also followed the King to hear the Dharma and make offerings.

Fourth: From the passage beginning with "At that time, Vaidehī saw the World-Honored One" down to "she became a member of Devadatta’s retinue," this section precisely clarifies how the lady raised her head to see the Buddha, lamenting aloud with deep-seated resentment.
Regarding the statement "she snapped her own necklace," this clarifies that although the lady’s body was adorned with necklaces, her attachment had not yet been eliminated;
upon suddenly seeing the Tathāgata, she felt such shame and remorse that she snapped them off herself.
Question:
"In what way does one cut oneself off? Answer:
"This lady is the most noble among the noble and the most honored among the honored; her four physical postures are attended by many, and all the garments she wears are provided by those around her."

"Now that she has seen the Buddha, her sense of shame and remorse is so profound that she does not rely on her belt or sash, but suddenly pulls herself away; thus it is said that she 'severed [herself] from it'.
As for the statement "she threw her entire body to the ground," this clarifies that the Lady’s inner feelings were so deeply moved by grief that her resentment and suffering became unbearable.
Therefore, he rose from his seat and stood up, and from standing, he leaped to the ground.
This was because his grief and resentment were so profound that he could no longer maintain the formalities of prostration and ritual decorum.
Regarding the phrase "wailing and crying out toward the Buddha," this clarifies that the lady rolled about before the Buddha, fainting and wailing aloud.

Regarding the passage beginning with "having addressed the Buddha," this clarifies that after the lady had rolled about, weeping and sobbing for some time, she finally regained partial consciousness; she then straightened her posture and demeanor, joined her palms, and addressed the Buddha:

"Since the beginning of my present life, I have never committed a great transgression. I do not know what karmic causes and conditions from past lives have brought such calamity upon me, such that I am a mother to this child?"
This illustrious lady, having long obstructed her own insight and being ignorant of her past causes, now perceives this child’s harm as an unexpected calamity.
I pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will show me the direct path.

The passage beginning with "The World-Honored One, what further causes and conditions... and following clarifies that the lady addressed her grievances to the Buddha, stating: "I am an ordinary person whose afflictions and delusions are not yet exhausted; that I have incurred this evil retribution is something I accept with a willing heart."

The World-Honored One has practiced the Way through vast eons; with both the correct and the habitual having perished, his manifold wisdoms are brilliantly clear, and his fruition being perfected, he is titled Buddha.
I do not yet understand by what causes and conditions he became a kinsman to Devadatta.
This intention has two aspects:
