first, to clarify that the queen harbored resentment toward her son and suddenly gave rise to a rebellious mind against her parents;
second, to clarify that she further resented Devadatta for instructing Ajātaśatru to devise this evil plot.
"If it were not for Deva, my son would never have had such an intention.
It is for this reason that I ask this question.
Furthermore, regarding the lady's question to the Buddha concerning Deva’s retinue, there are two [types]:
First are the lay relatives;
second are the monastic relatives.
Regarding the lay relatives, there were four who were the Buddha’s paternal uncles.
The Buddha was the son of King Śuddhodana.
Kapphiṇa was the son of King Śuklodana.
Devadatta was the son of King Droṇodana.
As for the son of Māra, he was the son of King Amṛtodana;
this is what is meant by "external lay retinue.
As for the "monastic retinue," they are called the "internal retinue" because they became disciples of the Buddha.
Although there have been four different sets of phrases above, this concludes the detailed explanation of the conditions for wearying of suffering.
Fifth, within the conditions for aspiring toward purity, there are eight parts.
First, from "I only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively explain for me" down to "in this turbid and evil world," this correctly clarifies the general request made by the Lady.
The separate designation of the realm of suffering clarifies that when a noble lady encounters the suffering of her own body, she realizes the world is impermanent;
it is the same for all six realms, where there is no ground for a mind at ease.
First, having heard the Buddha’s teaching on the birthless Pure Land, she vows to cast off this defiled body to realize the bliss of that unconditioned state.
Second, from the passage "from this turbid and evil place" down to "not seeing any more evil people," the text correctly clarifies that the Lady brings forth the objects of her aversion.
This clarifies that throughout Jambudvīpa there is nothing but evil, and not a single place worthy of attachment.
It is merely through delusion that fools drink in this long-lasting suffering.
To speak of this "turbid and evil realm" precisely elucidates the realm of suffering.
Furthermore, the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) is also the locus of the dependent retribution for sentient beings; it is likewise called the locus upon which sentient beings rely.
As for the mention of the hells and so forth below, these three grades of evil fruits are the most severe.
Regarding the term "overflowing," this mass of the three sufferings does not merely refer to Jambudvīpa alone; it exists everywhere throughout the Sahā world, and is thus said to be overflowing.

Regarding the term "a great mass of unwholesome [deeds]," this clarifies that within the three realms and six destinies, there are different types as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, distinguished according to the variations of the mind.
The Sūtra says:

"Karma can adorn consciousness; from life to life and place to place, each follows conditions toward its respective destination to receive retribution, such that those facing one another do not recognize each other.

Regarding the passage beginning with "I vow that in the future," this clarifies that the Lady’s true mind has reached its ultimate depth: she detests the suffering of Saṃsāra, delights in the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and seeks forever to return to eternal bliss.
However, the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) cannot be ascended with such ease;
this world of suffering and affliction (*saṃsāra*) cannot be left at will.
Unless one resolves to develop the adamantine will (*vajra-citta*) and forever sever the root of birth and death, there is no way out.
If one does not personally attend upon the Compassionate Honored One, how could one possibly overcome such long-drawn sighs?

However, my vow is that in the future I shall not hear evil sounds or encounter evil people; this clarifies that, like King Ajātaśatru and Devadatta—who killed their fathers and split the Saṃgha—I vow never to hear or see such things as their evil reputations.
Since King Śatānīka was his own biological son, yet he gave rise to the intent to kill his parents, how much more so would he harm those who are strangers?
For this reason, the lady did not distinguish between kin and stranger, but abandoned them all at once.

Third, from the passage "From now on, toward the World-Honored One" down to "having already repented," it clearly demonstrates that the Queen’s Pure Land is a wondrous place where those who have not cultivated goodness will not be born;
it is feared that there may be remaining transgressions that would obstruct her from going there.
Therefore, one must seek compassion and further perform repentance.

Fourth, from the passage beginning with "I only pray that the Buddha-sun... down to the section on "pure karma," it correctly clarifies the Queen’s general request for the departure [of the Bodhisattva].
This clarifies that the Lady previously requested [the Buddha] to reveal the place of rebirth; now she likewise requests [him to reveal] the practice by which one attains birth there.
The term "Buddha-sun" (buddhasūrya) is a dual designation, employing both a metaphor and its referent.
For example, when the sun rises, all darkness is dispelled.
So too, through the radiant light of the Buddha’s wisdom, the night of ignorance is made bright as day.

From the passage beginning with "Instructing me to contemplate purity" onwards, it correctly clarifies that once one is able to weary of the foul and rejoice in the pure, one can settle the mind and focus the thoughts so as to attain rebirth in a pure realm.

5. From the passage where the World-Honored One emits light from between his eyebrows down to the point where Vaidhīṣikā has seen it, this section precisely clarifies how the World-Honored One extensively manifests the Pure Land in response to her prior general request.

This clarifies that because the World-Honored One saw the Lady extensively seeking a pure land, the Tathāgata immediately emitted light from between his eyebrows to illuminate the lands of the ten directions; he gathered these lands with the light, which returned to his crown and transformed into a golden terrace as vast as Mount Sumeru.
The word "like" (ru) means "resembling. It resembles Mount Sumeru; this mountain is narrow at its waist and broad at the top, and all Buddha-lands appear within it.
They are variously different, with distinct adornments.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, everything became clear and distinct, and Vaidehī was enabled to see it all completely.
She asked:
"Vaidehī previously requested that you extensively describe for me the place free from sorrow; why does the Buddha not now describe it extensively?"
"What is the significance of the Golden Terrace appearing universally?
He replied,
"This reveals the profound mystery of the Tathāgata’s intention."

However, although Vaidehī’s words constitute a request that broadly opens the gateway to the Pure Land, were I to provide a general exposition of it, I fear she would fail to see its meaning and her mind would remain confused.
"Therefore, each [scene] appears individually before their eyes; they may believe in what they require and choose for themselves according to their own hearts.

6. From the passage where Vaidehī addresses the Buddha down to "all possess radiant light," this section precisely clarifies that the Lady presides over all that is manifested, feeling profound gratitude for the Buddha’s grace.
This clarifies that the Lady saw the Buddha-lands of the ten directions in their entirety, all of them exquisite.
Yet, when compared to the adornments of Sukhāvatī, they were entirely beyond comparison.
Therefore, she said: "I now wish to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss."
Question:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions are no different in their severing of delusions; since their practices are complete and their fruits are perfected, they too should be without distinction.
Why is it that within a single type of pure land there exists such superiority and inferiority?"
He replied:
"The Buddha is the Dharma King, whose supernatural powers are sovereign; whether he is superior or inferior is not something that can be known by the delusions of ordinary beings.

He manifests or remains hidden according to the capacities of sentient beings, with the sole aim of providing transformative benefit. Thus, it may be that his remaining hidden there is considered superior, while his manifesting alone in the Western Land is regarded as preeminent."
7. From "From now on, I shall joyfully give birth in the land of Amitābha" onwards, the text correctly clarifies that the Lady specifically chose her object of aspiration.
This explains the forty-eight vows of Amitābha’s original land, wherein each vow gives rise to a superior and most excellent cause.

Relying on causes, one gives rise to superior practice; relying on practice, one brings about superior fruition; relying on fruition, one brings about the accomplishment of superior retribution; relying on retribution, one brings about the accomplishment of ultimate bliss; relying on bliss, one manifests the penetration of compassionate transformation; and relying on compassionate transformation, one reveals and opens the gate of wisdom.
Yet compassion is inexhaustible and wisdom is likewise infinite.
When compassion and wisdom function in tandem, they extensively open the way to the nectar of immortality;
through this dharma-moisture, all sentient beings are universally gathered and sustained.

Other sutras offer many exhortations, and the various sages with one mind all point to and praise this; for these reasons, the Tathāgata secretly dispatched his consort to select [the candidate] separately.
8. From the passage beginning with "I only pray that the World-Honored One... onwards, it clearly explains the Queen’s request for a separate practice.

This clarifies that once Vaidehī had selected her place of rebirth, she returned to cultivate a distinct practice, exerting herself and focusing her mind, with the firm hope of benefiting others there.

To say "instruct me to contemplate" refers to the preparatory practices preceding meditative concentration (*samādhi*); it means to reflect upon and keep in mind the two types of retribution—the environment and its inhabitants—as well as the four kinds of adornments of that land.

Regarding the statement "teaching me right reception" (*samāpatti*): this clarifies that because of the preceding contemplations, the mental formations gradually become subtle until both perception and conceptualization vanish; there remains only the concentrated mind in union with the objective field, which is termed "right reception."
This has been briefly analyzed herein; it shall be further explained in detail below in the section on the gate of contemplation.
It should be understood that although there have been eight different phrases above, the extensive explanation of the conditions for aspiring toward purity is now complete.
Sixth, regarding the manifestation of the conditions for practice through mundane virtues, there are five parts.
First, from the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One immediately smiled" down to "he became an Anāgāmin," this section correctly clarifies how the light benefited the King, his father.

This clarifies that because the Tathāgata saw that the lady wished to be reborn in Sukhāvatī and further requested the practice for such rebirth, he acted in accordance with his own fundamental intent and manifested the original vow of Amitābha; through these two requests, he extensively opened the gateway to the Pure Land.
It is not only Vaidehī who departs; all sentient beings who hear this will go as well.
Because there is such benefit, the Tathāgata smiles.

As for the statement that light of five colors issues from the Buddha’s mouth, this clarifies that it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the constant majestic demeanor of the minds and mouths of all Buddhas that whatever light they emit must necessarily bring benefit.

Regarding the statement that each ray of light shines upon King Bimbisāra’s crown, this precisely clarifies that the light from the Buddha’s mouth does not illuminate other directions, but shines only upon the king’s crown.
Nevertheless, wherever the Buddha’s light emanates from his body, it invariably brings benefit.
The Buddha emitted light from beneath his feet, which illuminated and benefited the realm of hell-beings.
If the light issued from his knees, it illuminated and benefited the realm of animals.
If the light issued from his private organ, it illuminated and benefited the realm of hungry ghosts.
If the light issues from the navel, it illuminates and benefits the realm of asuras.
If the light issues from the heart, it illuminates and benefits the realm of humans.
If the light issues from the mouth, it illuminates and benefits those of the two vehicles.
If light were to issue from between his eyebrows, it would illuminate those who further the Mahāyāna.
Now, to clarify that this light issues from his mouth and shines directly upon the king’s crown, it signifies that he is being granted the Lesser Fruit (śrāvaka-phala).
If the light issues from between the eyebrows and enters through the crown of the Buddha’s head, it signifies that the Bodhisattva has been granted a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Such meanings are vast and immeasurable, and cannot be fully recounted.

The passage beginning with "At that time, although the Great King was in confinement" and following clearly explains how the Father King’s crown was illuminated by light, whereby his mental eye opened; despite the many intervening barriers, they naturally beheld one another.
This was seeing the Buddha by means of the light, which was not what she had anticipated.
By paying homage and taking refuge, she immediately transcended to realize the third fruit [of the śrotāpanna].

Second, from the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to the extensive explanation of various parables, the text correctly clarifies the answer to the former lady’s specific request regarding the practice she sought.

This clarifies that from the time the Tathāgata descended from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and entered the royal palace until this point in the text, the World-Honored One sat in silence, having not yet spoken at all.

However, as for the Queen’s repentance and inquiry, the emission of light, the manifestation of the [Pure] Land, and so forth—these were events that Ānanda witnessed at the Buddha’s royal palace. Once the matter was concluded, he returned to the mountain and recounted these aforementioned events to the great assembly at Gṛdhrakūṭa; it is from this that the present text first originated.
Furthermore, it should be understood that these words are not uttered by the Buddha at no particular time.
One should know that from the passage beginning "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Vaidehī" onwards, he is formally granting his command and permitting the teaching.
Regarding the statement that Amitābha Buddha is not far away, this precisely clarifies the objective realm for fixing the mind, which consists of three aspects.
First, it clarifies the spatial limit of "not being far": from here, by passing beyond ten trillion *kṣetras*, one reaches the land of Amitābha.
Second, although the distance is vast, one arrives at the moment of departure through a single thought-instant.

Third, when Vaidehī and other sentient beings with karmic affinity focus their minds on visualization, they accord with the state of meditative concentration; thus, the practitioner naturally perceives it constantly.
Because there are these three meanings, it is said that [the Pure Land] is not far away.

Regarding the passage beginning with "You should fix your mindfulness," it correctly clarifies that ordinary delusions obstruct the profound mind and cause much distraction; if one does not immediately abandon攀緣 (pān-yuán, objective clinging), there is no way for the pure realm to manifest.
This refers to the correct teaching on settling the mind through abiding and practicing; if one relies upon this method, it is called the accomplishment of pure karma.

As for the passage beginning with "I now [speak] for you," this clarifies that when the conditions and capacities (*mārga-pratyaya*) are not yet complete, one must not unilaterally expound the gate of meditative concentration (*samādhi-mukha*).
The Buddha further observes the capacities [of sentient beings] and spontaneously opens up the practice of the three types of merit.

From the passage beginning with "Third, from [the section] 'also for those in future ages' down to 'the Land of Ultimate Bliss,'" it correctly clarifies the presentation of the capacities [of practitioners], the exhortation to cultivate [merit], and the attainment of benefits.
This clarifies that the benefits requested by the Lady are even more profound, and that those who in the future turn their minds [toward the Way] will all arrive there.

Fourth, from the passage beginning with "Those who wish to be born in that land" down to "is called pure karma," it correctly explains the exhortation to practice the three types of meritorious deeds.
This clarifies that the capacities of all sentient beings are of two kinds:
first, the concentrated; second, the distracted.

If one were to rely solely on the practice of concentration, it would fail to encompass all beings. Therefore, the Tathāgata, through skillful means, reveals and opens up the three types of merit to correspond to those with distracted faculties.
The phrase "those who wish to be born in that land" indicates the destination to which one is directed.
The phrase "one should cultivate the three blessings" provides a general outline of the gates of practice.
What are these three?
The first is filial support of one’s parents, which consists of four points.
First, regarding "filially supporting one’s parents": this clarifies that all ordinary beings are born dependent upon conditions.
What is meant by "relying on conditions"?
There are those born by transformation, those born from moisture, those born from eggs, and those born from a womb.
Within each of these four modes of birth, there are further four modes of birth, as explained at length in the sutras; however, wherever there is birth through mutual dependence, there are parents.

Since one possesses both parents, there is great kindness; for if there were no father, the cause by which one is born would be lacking, and if there were no mother, the condition by which one is born would be discordant. If both were absent, the ground for taking birth would be lost; it is only when the conditions of both parents are complete that there is a place to receive a body.

When one is about to receive a body, one's own karmic consciousness acts as the internal cause, while the semen and blood of the parents act as the external conditions; through the conjunction of these causes and conditions, this body comes to be. For this reason, the kindness of one's parents is profound.

When the mother has been pregnant for ten months, she constantly experiences suffering and distress in her walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; furthermore, she fears the difficulty of death during childbirth.
Once the child is born, it remains constantly sleeping in excrement and urine for three years, such that its bedding, covers, and clothing are likewise impure.

When they have grown up and, out of love for their wives and affection for their children, instead give rise to hatred and resentment toward their parents and fail to practice kindness and filial piety, they are no different from animals.
Furthermore, parents are the ultimate field of merit within the world.
The Buddha is the ultimate field of merit that transcends the world.

Yet, when the Buddha was in the world, he encountered a time of famine; people were all dying of starvation, white bones lay scattered everywhere, and it was difficult for the bhikṣus to obtain almsfood.

At that time, after the bhikṣus had departed, the World-Honored One entered the city alone to beg for food. From dawn until midday, he called out at every gate for alms, but no one gave him food; the Buddha returned with his bowl empty.
The next day he went again, but could not find him; on the following day he went once more, yet still could not find him.
Suddenly, a bhikṣu encountered the Buddha on the road; his complexion was unusual, appearing as though he were hungry. The bhikṣu immediately asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
“Have you already finished eating?
The Buddha said, “Bhikṣu, for three days now I have been unable to obtain even a single spoonful of alms-food. I am currently famished and devoid of strength; I can hardly speak with you.”
Having heard the Buddha’s words, the bhikṣu was overcome with tears of grief and could not restrain himself; he then thought to himself:

“The Buddha is the unsurpassed field of merit and the protector of all sentient beings. I shall sell these three robes of mine and purchase a bowl of rice to offer to the Buddha; now is the very time for this.”
Having had this thought, he immediately purchased a bowl of rice and hurriedly brought it to the Buddha.
The Buddha, knowing the situation, asked him intentionally:
"Bhikṣu, during this year of famine when people are all dying of hunger, from where have you now obtained this bowl of pure-colored rice?"
The bhikṣu reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One as before.
The Buddha spoke again:

“Bhikṣu, these three robes are the banner and sign of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. The causes and conditions of these robes are most honored, most weighty, and most gracious. That you have now easily obtained this food and offered it to me—this greatly rewards your kind intention; I cannot consume this food.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha again with urgency:
"The Buddha is the field of merit for the three realms and the pinnacle among the sages; if even You say that it cannot be digested, who else besides the Buddha could digest it?"
The Buddha said,
"Bhikṣu, do you have parents? He replied:
"There is. "Take this to offer to your parents.
The bhikṣu said:
"If even the Buddha said it could not be digested, how could my parents possibly digest it?
The Buddha said,
"They can digest it."
"Why is this? Because one's parents can give birth to one's body and have bestowed upon one great and profound kindness; for this reason, [the offense] may be extinguished.
The Buddha again asked the bhikṣu:
"Do your parents have faith in the Buddha?
The bhikṣu replied,
"They have no faith at all."
The Buddha said:
"Now there is one with faith.
Seeing you give me food, he felt great joy; because of this, he has immediately given rise to faith."
"First teach them to receive the Three Refuges, and they will then be able to digest this food.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having received the Buddha’s instruction with deep reverence, departed.
For this reason, one must provide great filial support and care for one's parents.
Furthermore, after the Buddha’s mother, Māyā, gave birth to the Buddha, she passed away seven days later and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

After the Buddha attained enlightenment, on the fifteenth day of the fourth month, he ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for one summer retreat to preach the Dharma for his mother, in order to repay the kindness of her ten-month pregnancy.
If even the Buddha himself received and repaid the kindness of his parents through filial support, how much more so should ordinary people practice filial piety?
Thus, one knows that the debt of gratitude owed to one's parents is profoundly deep and extremely heavy.

As for serving one's teachers and elders, this clarifies the instruction on ritual propriety: by learning and cultivating virtue, and acting without deficiency until the attainment of Buddhahood, all of this is due to the power of the teacher as a virtuous friend.
This great kindness must be most deeply revered; indeed, honoring one's parents, teachers, and elders is what is called "the practice of reverent conduct.
As for the statement regarding "loving-kindness and abstaining from killing," this clarifies that all sentient beings take their lives as their very foundation.
If one sees unfavorable conditions and flees in fear, seeking shelter and concealment, it is solely for the sake of protecting one's life.
As the Sūtra says:
"All sentient beings without exception cherish their own lives; do not kill, do not wield the staff, and use yourself as a metaphor for others."
This is precisely what constitutes realization.
Regarding the statement "to cultivate the ten wholesome actions," this clarifies that among the ten unwholesome actions, the act of killing is the most evil; therefore, it is listed first.
Among the ten wholesome actions, longevity is the most excellent; therefore, it is used here as a counterpart.
As for the nine unwholesome and nine wholesome actions mentioned below, they shall be described in detail later in the section on the nine grades.
This clarifies mundane goodness, which is also called the "inferior practice of loving-kindness.
Second, regarding the phrase "receiving and upholding the Three Refuges," this clarifies that such mundane goodness is slight and its resulting retribution is incomplete.
The majesty of the virtue of the precepts is capable of evoking the fruit of Bodhi.
However, sentient beings turn to faith from the shallow to the deep:
first they receive the Three Refuges, and subsequently they are taught the various precepts.

Regarding the phrase "endowed with all precepts": there are many kinds of precepts, such as the three-refuge precepts, the five precepts, the eight precepts, the ten wholesome precepts, the two hundred and twenty precepts, the five hundred precepts, the śrāmaṇera precepts, or the bodhisattva’s three clusters of pure precepts and the ten inexhaustible precepts; therefore, it is called being "endowed with all precepts."
Furthermore, within each category of precepts, there are also minor precepts, major precepts, and complete precepts.

Regarding the statement "not violating the rules of decorum," this clarifies that the actions of body, speech, and mind—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—are able to serve as the skillful means and decorum for all precepts.
Whether light or heavy, coarse or subtle, one is able to maintain them all.
Upon transgressing, one immediately repents; therefore, it is said that one does not violate the rules of decorum.
This is called the goodness of precepts (*śīla-kuśala*).
Third, regarding the phrase "generating the bodhicitta": this clarifies that sentient beings should aspire with joy toward the Great Vehicle; one must not generate a shallow, minor cause.
Were it not for the extensive generation of the vast mind, how could one possibly encounter Bodhi?
I only pray that my body may become identical with empty space and my mind equal to the Dharma-realm, exhausting the nature of all sentient beings.
With my physical actions, I shall reverently make offerings, prostrate, welcome and escort them as they come and go, and transport them until all are saved.

Furthermore, by means of my verbal karma, I praise and extol the preaching of the Dharma; all who receive my transformation are led to the exhaustion of suffering, with none failing to attain the Way upon hearing my words.

Moreover, by means of my mental karma, I enter meditative concentration to observe and manifest throughout the Dharma-realm, delivering beings according to their capacities, leaving not a single one unredeemed.

I have made this vow, which increases with every passing moment like space, pervading everywhere without exception; its flow of practice is inexhaustible, reaching to the very end of time, such that my body never tires and my mind never knows satiety.
Furthermore, "bodhi" is a name for the fruit of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, "mind" refers to the mind of sentient beings that is capable of seeking.
Therefore, it is called "generating the bodhicitta."
Fourth, regarding the phrase "profoundly believing in cause and effect," there are two aspects.

First, to clarify the causes and effects of worldly suffering and happiness: if one creates the cause of suffering, one will experience the fruit of suffering; if one creates the cause of happiness, one will experience the fruit of happiness. This is like pressing a seal into clay—the impression is formed as soon as the seal is removed; of this, one must not doubt.
Regarding the phrase "reciting and studying the Mahāyāna," this clarifies that the scriptural teachings are like a mirror.
By reading and investigating them repeatedly, one develops wisdom.
Once the eye of wisdom is opened, one is then able to grow weary of suffering and rejoice in the bliss of Nirvāṇa.

Regarding the phrase "exhorting toward progress," this clarifies that the nature of suffering is like poison and unwholesome dharmas are like knives; they cause harm to sentient beings as they circulate through the three realms of existence.
Now, since goodness is like a clear mirror and the Dharma is like nectar.
The mirror reflects the Right Path to lead one back to the Truth; the nectar pours down the rain of Dharma without exhaustion.
Desiring that all sentient beings receive its moisture and equally join the flow of the Dharma, for these reasons, we must exhort one another.
The passage following "Having spoken thus of these three matters" concludes by synthesizing them into the aforementioned practices.
Fifth, from "The Buddha addressed Vaidehī" down to "the direct cause," it clarifies how he draws upon the sages to encourage ordinary beings.
Provided one can focus the mind with determination, one will certainly proceed without doubt.
Although there have been five different points above, this concludes the extensive explanation of the conditions for the practice of dispersed goodness (*vikṣiptakuśala*).
Seven: Regarding the demonstration of the conditions for contemplation within the meditative goodness, there are seven parts.
First, from "The Buddha addressed Ānanda" down to "pure karma," this correctly clarifies the command to listen and the permission to speak.
This clarifies that Vajrapāṇi previously requested to be reborn in Sukhāvatī and further requested the practice by which such birth could be attained; the Tathāgata has already granted this.
Now, based on this text, the intention is precisely to reveal the skillful means for attaining correct meditative absorption (*samyak-samādhi*).
This is a matter of supreme importance regarding causes and conditions, and its benefit is profound.
It has been rare to hear of such a thing throughout vast eons, yet it is only now being spoken.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has commanded both individuals together.
As for saying "I address Ānanda": I now wish to open and expound the gate of the Pure Land; you must uphold it well and ensure it is not lost.

As for saying "I address Vaidehī": you are the one who requested this Dharma; I now wish to speak it, so you must listen attentively, reflect upon it, and receive it with precision, ensuring no error or omission occurs.

Regarding the statement "for all sentient beings of future ages," it is because the Tathāgata, when manifesting his transformative power, has focused primarily on those sentient beings who are perpetually submerged; now that he has spread the compassionate clouds equally, he hopes that all may be moistened by the coming rain.
Regarding the statement that speech is harmed by the thieves of afflictions, this clarifies that ordinary beings have heavy obstructions and deep delusions of false attachment.

They do not realize that the fiery pits of the three evil realms lie beneath their very feet; yet, as they act in accordance with conditions, they intend to use these actions as provisions for advancing on the Path.
How is it that the six thieves have taken notice and vied with one another to invade and seize?
Now that these treasures of the Dharma have been lost, how could there not be sorrow and suffering?

Regarding the statement on "pure karma," this clarifies that because the Tathāgata perceives the transgressions of sentient beings, he teaches them the methods for repentance, desiring to cause their continuity to be severed and eliminated, so that they may ultimately and forever be purified.

Furthermore, regarding what is called "purity": by relying on the lower gate of contemplation, one focuses the mind on the Buddha and directs one's thoughts toward the Western Land; as every thought-moment eliminates transgressions, it is therefore pure.
Second, from "Excellent! onwards, it correctly clarifies the lady's inquiry regarding the Sage’s intention.

Third, from "Ānanda, you should receive and uphold this" onwards, until "having proclaimed the Buddha’s words," it correctly clarifies the exhortation to uphold and the exhortation to proclaim this profound and essential Dharma, which must be widely disseminated.

This clarifies that the Tathāgata first gave a general instruction to settle the mind and listen with receptivity; this passage, however, specifically commands Ānanda to receive and uphold it without forgetting, and to expound and circulate it in places where many people gather.

Regarding the phrase "the Buddha’s words," this clarifies that the Tathāgata has long since eliminated all verbal faults over the course of vast eons; thus, whatever he utters, all who hear it naturally give rise to faith.

4. From the passage beginning with "The Tathāgata now... down to "...having attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)," this section correctly clarifies the characteristics of the benefits gained through the exhortation to practice.

This explains that the Tathāgata, for the sake of the lady [Vaidehī] and others in the future, reveals the skillful means of contemplation: focusing the mind on the Western Land, abandoning weariness with the Sahā world, and joyfully aspiring toward Sukhāvatī.

The passage beginning with "By the power of the Buddha" clarifies that the karmic obstructions of sentient beings cause them to be born blind at the mere sight of things; they mistake their fingers and palms for distant lands, and what is separated from them by a bamboo mat in another direction they perceive as being a thousand li away.
How much more so for ordinary beings to peer into the minds within the realm of the Buddhas! Were it not for the secret empowerment of the Sage’s power, by what means could that land be beheld?

The passage beginning with "It is like holding up a bright mirror and seeing one's own facial reflection" clarifies that when the Lady and all sentient beings enter contemplation and abide in their minds, concentrating their spirits without distraction, the mind and its objects correspond and everything becomes manifest. When the objects appear before them, it is no different from seeing things within a mirror.

Regarding the statement that one attains patience because the mind is joyful: this clarifies that when the pure light of Amitābha Buddha’s land suddenly appears before one's eyes, how could one not leap for joy?
Because of this joy, one immediately attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*); it is also called the patience of joy, the patience of awakening, and the patience of faith.
This is an abstruse discourse; the specific stage at which it is attained has not yet been indicated.
To cause the noble ladies and others to aspire to this benefit, they should only realize patience (*kṣānti*) when they perceive it through diligent and focused mental visualization.
This is mostly the patience within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), not the patience above the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*).
5. From the passage beginning with "The Buddha said to Vaidehī" down to "enabling you to behold it," it clearly demonstrates that the Lady was an ordinary person and not a sage.
Because she was not a sage, she could behold that land despite its great distance by relying on the secret empowerment of the Sage’s power.
This clarifies that the Tathāgata feared sentient beings would remain in delusion, claiming that a noblewoman is a saint and not an ordinary person.
Because such doubts arise, they themselves become timid and weak.
However, although Vaidehī is actually a bodhisattva manifesting in the guise of an ordinary body,
we sinners have no means by which to equal her.
To sever this doubt, he said, "You are an ordinary person."
Regarding the statement that her thoughts and mind were weak and inferior: because she was an ordinary person, she had never possessed great resolve.

Regarding the statement that she had not yet attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*): this clarifies that the Lady’s physical eyes (*māṃsacakṣus*)—and the distance they could perceive—are not even worth mentioning.
How much more so for the Pure Land, which is exceedingly remote; how can it be seen?

From the passage beginning "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have various skillful means" onwards, this clarifies that if the adornments of the lands seen according to one's own mind were not universally accessible to you ordinary beings, it would be entirely due to the merit of the Buddha.

Sixth: From the passage where Vaidhī addresses the Buddha down to the point where she has beheld that land, it clarifies how the Lady reiterates her previous gratitude in order to give rise to the intent for her subsequent questions.

This clarifies that the Lady understood the Buddha’s intention; she had previously regarded what she saw upon the radiant terrace as her own capability, but now, having witnessed the World-Honored One’s instruction, she finally realized it was the grace of the Buddha’s skillful means.
If that is so, while the Buddha is currently in the world, sentient beings may receive his mindful protection and thus be able to see the Western [Pure Land].
But if the Buddha enters nirvana and no longer bestows such grace, how could they possibly see it?

Seventh: From the passage beginning with "If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa... down to "...the world of Ultimate Bliss," it correctly clarifies that the Lady, out of compassion for sentient beings, resolved to be reborn there together with them, forever departing from Saṃhā and traveling eternally to the Land of Peace and Bliss.
This clarifies that the Tathāgata’s aspiration to deliver beings extends through the furthest reaches of the future without ceasing.

However, because the times have shifted across generations and the dispositions of the multitudes have become shallow and short-sighted, the Tathāgata has shortened his eternally existing lifespan and condensed long kalpas into human years; he has restrained pride to demonstrate impermanence and transformed those of stubborn nature so they may together return to extinction.
Therefore, it says, "if after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the phrase "all sentient beings," this clarifies that when the Tathāgata has ceased his transformative activity, sentient beings have no place of refuge.
They are writhing and bewildered, running hither and thither through the six realms of existence.
Regarding the phrase "turbid, evil, and unwholesome," this clarifies the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*):

first, the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*); second, the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*); third, the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*); fourth, the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*); and fifth, the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).

Regarding what is called the "impurity of the eon" (kalpa-kaṣāya): the eon itself is not inherently impure; rather, it becomes so when the eon is in its period of decline, as all manner of evils increase.
Regarding what is called the "impurity of sentient beings" (sattva-kaṣāya): when the eon first begins to form, sentient beings are purely virtuous;
when the eon reaches its end, the ten non-virtuous actions of sentient beings flourish ever more intensely.
Regarding the "impurity of views" (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*): one's own various evils are collectively transformed into goodness, yet regarding others, there is nothing that is not viewed as wrong.

Regarding the "impurity of afflictions" (*kleśa-kaṣāya*): at the end of this present kalpa, sentient beings are of evil nature and difficult to approach; in response to the six sense faculties, greed and anger arise in competition.

Regarding the "impurity of lifespan": due to the two preceding impurities of views and afflictions, beings frequently engage in killing and lack compassionate care. Since they have committed the causes for the suffering of ending life while desiring the fruit of a long life, by what means could such a result possibly be obtained?
However, that which is turbid is by nature not wholesome.
This concludes the brief indication of the meaning of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
As for the phrase "oppressed by the five sufferings":

From among the eight sufferings, one takes the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, and the suffering of separation from what is loved; these are called the five sufferings.
When the [other] three sufferings are added, they constitute the eight sufferings.

First is the suffering of the five aggregates being in full bloom; second is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; third is the suffering of encountering those one hates; these together are called the eight sufferings.

These five turbidities, the five sufferings, the eight sufferings, and so forth, are experienced throughout the six realms of existence; there is no one who is exempt from them, as they constantly oppress and afflict all beings.
If one does not undergo this suffering, then one is not included among the ranks of ordinary beings.
As for the passage beginning with "How then shall one see," etc., this clarifies that the lady has raised up the catalyst for suffering.
These karmic offenses are extremely deep; furthermore, one has not seen the Buddha nor received his protective empowerment. How, then, can one see that land?
Although there have been seven different phrases above, this concludes the extensive explanation of the wholesome meditative states, demonstrating the conditions for contemplation.
First, the sequence for verifying faith is elucidated; next, the sequence prior to the transformation is elucidated; finally, the sequence of the incitement is elucidated.
Although there have been these three different sequences above, the exposition of the introductory section as a whole is now complete.
