Eleventh, there are distinct benefits obtained after the bright flowers have opened.
Regarding the meaning of these eleven gates, they are established in relation to the text on the nine grades.
Within each individual grade, all eleven [gates] are present; thus, this constitutes one hundred points of meaning.

Furthermore, the meaning of these eleven gates may be summarized and analyzed prior to the passage concerning the superior class, or it may be analyzed individually prior to the passages concerning the middle and lower classes.
Furthermore, if this meaning is examined according to the textual records, there are instances where it is complete and instances where it is incomplete;
although there are thus hidden and manifest variations, according to the underlying principle, it should be present in all cases.
For this reason, it is necessary to extensively expound and clarify [the meaning], desiring that those who rely on this practice may easily understand and recognize it.
Although there have been eleven different sections above, the detailed analysis of the meaning and intent of the three grades of the superior class is now complete.
Next, regarding the section on the "Highest Birth in the Highest Grade," it likewise first presents the heading, then provides the exposition, and finally offers the conclusion;
this consists of twelve parts.
First, from the point where the Buddha addresses Ānanda onwards, two intentions are presented together as headings.
First, it clarifies the proclamation of the mandate;
second, it clarifies the determination of their station.
These are the ordinary persons of superior goodness who practice and study the Mahāyāna.
3. From the passage beginning with "If there are sentient beings" down to "they will immediately be reborn," this correctly clarifies the general enumeration of all classes of living beings.
There are four such categories.
First, clarifying the person capable of faith;
second, clarifying the aspiration for rebirth;
third, clarifying the extent of the resolve.
The fourth clarifies the benefit of attaining birth [in that land].
From "From what three... downwards, up to "...will certainly be born in that land," it correctly clarifies and determines the three minds as the direct cause.
There are two points here:

first, it clarifies that the World-Honored One’s intention in manifesting benefits according to the capacities of beings is subtle and difficult to discern; unless the Buddha himself were to pose the questions and inquiries, there would be no way to attain understanding.
Second, it clarifies that the Tathāgata himself answers the number of the three preceding minds.
The Sūtra says: "First is the sincere mind. "Ultimate" (*zhi*) means true; "sincere" (*cheng*) means real.

This clarifies that the practice and understanding cultivated through the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of all sentient beings must be performed from within a truly real mind. One must not outwardly manifest the appearance of being virtuous, good, and diligent while inwardly harboring falsehood, greed, hatred, deviance, hypocrisy, and a hundred forms of craftiness. Such an evil nature is difficult to approach, resembling a snake or a scorpion. Although one may initiate the three types of action, it is called "poisoned goodness" and is termed "false conduct"; it is not called "true karma."

If one practices by settling the mind in this manner, even if they exert themselves with body and mind to the utmost, running and working with urgency throughout the twelve periods of day and night like one whose head is on fire, it is merely a "good" that is mixed with various poisons.
If one wishes to turn back from these practices mixed with poison and seek birth in that Buddha’s Pure Land, this is absolutely impossible.

Why is this? It is precisely because when Amitābha Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path in his causal stage, even down to a single thought-moment or a single kṣaṇa, all that he cultivated through the three karmas was performed within a mind of absolute sincerity; whatever actions he undertook and whatever he sought were likewise entirely sincere.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of reality:
first, the reality of self-benefit;
second, the reality of benefiting others.
Regarding what is called the reality of self-benefit, there are further two kinds.

First, within a mind of reality, one restrains and abandons all evils and defilements of oneself and others, as well as impure lands and the like; whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one maintains the thought that one is identical to all bodhisattvas in restraining and abandoning all evils, thinking, "I am also thus."
Second, within a mind of true reality, diligently cultivate the virtues of oneself and others, both ordinary and holy;
and within a mind of true reality, perform verbal karma by praising that Amitābha Buddha and his two rewards—the primary body and the environment.

Furthermore, within the mind of ultimate reality, one’s verbal karma consists of disparaging and detesting the suffering and evils of the three realms and six paths—the dual retributions of self and others, both the physical environment and its inhabitants—and likewise praising the wholesome deeds performed by the three karmas of all sentient beings; as for those actions that are not wholesome, one respects them from afar and does not rejoice in them.

Furthermore, with a mind of ultimate reality, there is the physical karma of joining the palms in prostration and making offerings through the four types of service to that Amitābha Buddha and his two-fold retribution—the environment and the inhabitants.

Moreover, with a mind of ultimate reality, there is the physical karma of treating this triple world of birth and death, including both self and others and their two-fold retribution—the environment and the inhabitants—with contempt, weariness, and renunciation.

Furthermore, within the mind of true reality, the mental karma consists of contemplating and observing that Amitābha Buddha and his two-fold retribution—the primary and the secondary—as if they were present before one's eyes.

Furthermore, within the mind of ultimate reality, the mental karma that feels contempt for and seeks to abandon this cycle of birth and death, the three realms, and the two types of retribution—both self and others, as well as the support and the supported—must necessarily be abandoned from within the mind of ultimate reality. These unwholesome three karmas must be relinquished from within the mind of ultimate reality.

Furthermore, if one gives rise to the three types of wholesome karma, they must be performed from within a state of genuine mind; regardless of whether the action is internal or external, manifest or hidden, it must all be authentic. Therefore, this is called the mind of utmost sincerity.
Second is the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*). What is called the "profound mind" is the mind of deep faith.
It also has two types.

The first is the resolute deep faith that one's own present self is an evil, ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), who for kalpas beyond measure has always been submerged and constantly transmigrating, without any conditions for liberation.

Second, one must have firm and resolute faith that Amitābha Buddha’s forty-eight vows embrace all sentient beings; free from doubt and hesitation, one will certainly attain rebirth by virtue of the power of those vows.

Furthermore, one must develop firm and resolute faith that the Buddha Śākyamuni taught these three blessings and nine grades of the *Contemplation Sūtra*—both the concentrated and the dispersed good deeds—to testify to and praise the two types of retribution, the primary and secondary, of that Buddha, thereby causing people to aspire to them with joy.

Furthermore, one must have firm and resolute faith that, as testified and exhorted by the Buddhas of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, all ordinary beings will certainly attain birth [in the Pure Land].

Furthermore, those with deep faith should aspire that all practitioners, with a single mind, believe only in the Buddha’s words; disregarding even their own bodies and lives, they shall resolutely practice in accordance with them.

When the Buddha commands one to abandon something, one abandons it; when the Buddha commands one to practice something, one practices it; when the Buddha commands one to go to a certain place, one goes there. This is called following the Buddha’s teaching and following the Buddha’s intention; this is called following the Buddha’s vow; this is called a true disciple of the Buddha.
Furthermore, all practitioners who rely solely on this sutra and practice with deep faith will certainly not lead sentient beings astray.
Why is this? Because the Buddha is one whose great compassion is perfected and because he speaks the truth.

Excluding the Buddha, those whose wisdom and practice are not yet perfected remain on the stage of learning (*śaikṣabhūmi*); because they have not yet eliminated the two obstacles of active afflictions and habitual tendencies, their fruition and vows are not yet complete.

Such ordinary beings and sages, even if they attempt to fathom the intent of the Buddha’s teachings, cannot reach a definitive understanding. Although they may offer discussions, they must still request the Buddha to certify them as being settled in truth.

If it accords with the Buddha’s intention, one may seal it by saying, "So it is, so it is. If it does not accord with the Buddha’s intention, one should say, "The meaning you have explained is not thus."
That which is not sealed [by the Buddha] is equivalent to neutral speech—speech that is neither beneficial nor advantageous.
That which the Buddha seals with approval is that which accords with the Buddha’s true teaching (*saddharma*).

If the Buddha’s every utterance constitutes the true teaching, the true meaning, right practice, right understanding, right action, and right wisdom, then whether it be much or little, the assembly shall not question whether it is right or wrong, regardless of whether they are bodhisattvas, humans, devas, or others.
One should know that what the Buddha has spoken is the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*), whereas everything spoken by bodhisattvas and others is termed the non-definitive teaching (*neyārtha*).

Therefore, I now respectfully exhort all those with the karmic affinity for rebirth: you must have deep faith in the Buddha’s words and practice them with single-minded devotion. You must not rely on the inconsistent teachings of bodhisattvas and others as grounds for doubt or obstruction; do not harbor delusions or fall into self-deception, thereby forfeiting the great benefit of rebirth.

Furthermore, one who possesses deep faith with a profound mind establishes their own mind with certainty, practices in accordance with the teachings, and forever eliminates doubt and error; they are not caused to fall away or be shaken by any divergent interpretations, divergent practices, heterodox studies, divergent views, or divergent attachments.
Question:

"Ordinary beings possess shallow wisdom while the obstacles of their delusions are deep. If they encounter many people with differing interpretations and practices who cite various scriptures and treatises to raise objections and difficulties—arguing that ordinary beings with all manner of karmic hindrances cannot attain rebirth there—how should one respond?"
"How does one counter such objections, achieve faith, proceed with certainty and directness, and avoid becoming discouraged or retreating?
He replied:
"If someone cites many scriptures and treatises as evidence that [rebirth] does not occur, the practitioner should respond: "
"Virtuous One, although you bring the sūtras and śāstras to testify that [all things] are unarisen, according to my own understanding, I certainly do not accept your refutation. Why is this?
It is not that I lack faith in those various sūtras and śāstras; indeed, I have full faith in them all."
However, when the Buddha spoke that sūtra, the location was distinct, the time was distinct, the audience was distinct, and the benefit was distinct.
Furthermore, the time he spoke that sūtra was not the same time he spoke the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, and so forth.

However, while the Buddha’s teachings were comprehensive in accommodating various capacities and the times were likewise diverse— those [other teachings] generally expounded the understanding and practice of humans,

devas, and bodhisattvas— the present *Contemplation Sūtra* teaches the two types of wholesome conduct, the meditative and the non-meditative, specifically for the sake of beings such as Vaidehī, as well as all ordinary persons in the five turbidities and five sufferings after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, attesting that they shall attain birth [in the Pure Land].

For this reason, I now single-mindedly rely upon this Buddha’s teaching and shall resolutely practice it; even if you were to speak of non-arising hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of times, it would only serve to increase and perfect my faith in rebirth [in the Pure Land].
Furthermore, the practitioner again says to the interlocutor:
"Virtuous one, listen well. I shall now further explain for you the characteristics of definitive faith.

Even if Bodhisattvas prior to the stages, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and others—whether individually or in great numbers, even filling the ten directions—all were to cite sūtras and śāstras as proof that [the Buddha] is not born, I would not give rise to a single thought of doubt; rather, my pure faith alone would increase and be perfected."
Why is this? Because the words of the Buddha are definitively established as definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and thus cannot be subverted by anyone.
Furthermore, if a practitioner listens well, even if those from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage—whether one or many, even filling the ten directions—should speak with one voice:

"If Śākyamuni Buddha praised Amitābha while disparaging the three realms and the six paths of rebirth, and exhorted sentient beings to single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name and cultivate other virtues so that they would certainly be reborn in that land after this present life ends—this must be false and cannot be relied upon as true."
"Although I have heard these various explanations, not even a single thought of doubt has arisen within me; rather, it only serves to increase and perfect my resolute and supreme faith."
Why is this? It is because the Buddha’s words are true and definitive in meaning.
The Buddha possesses actual knowledge, actual understanding, actual vision, and actual realization; his words do not arise from a mind of doubt.
Furthermore, they cannot be subverted by the divergent views or interpretations of other bodhisattvas; if one is truly a bodhisattva, the assembly will not contradict the Buddha’s teaching.

Setting this matter aside for a moment, the practitioner should know that even if transformation Buddhas or reward Buddhas—whether one or many, even to the point of filling the ten directions—each were to emit radiant light and extend their tongues to cover the ten directions, and each were to say:

"That which Śākyamuni has taught regarding the marks of praise and exhortation for all ordinary beings to single-mindedly recollect the Buddha, cultivate other virtues, and vow to be reborn in that Pure Land is false; such a thing certainly does not exist."

"Although I have heard these teachings spoken by all these Buddhas, I ultimately do not give rise to even a single thought of doubt or retreat, fearing that I might fail to be born in those Buddha-lands."

Why is this? Because for all Buddhas—whether one or many—their knowledge and vision, their understanding and practice, their realization and the fruit of their awakening, and their great compassion are identical and without the slightest difference. Therefore, what is established by one Buddha is established as such by all Buddhas.

Just as the Buddhas of the past established the prohibitions against killing and the ten non-virtuous actions, one who ultimately refrains from committing or practicing them is said to be engaged in the ten virtuous actions and the ten practices, which accord with the meaning of the six perfections.
If a future Buddha were to appear in the world, how could he possibly alter the ten wholesome deeds previously established to instead practice the ten unwholesome deeds?
By examining this principle through reasoning, it is clearly understood that the words and deeds of all Buddhas do not contradict one another.

Even if Śākyamuni were to point and exhort all ordinary beings to focus their mindfulness and practice exclusively throughout this single lifetime, such that upon the end of life they would certainly be reborn in that land, then all the Buddhas of the ten directions would likewise praise, exhort, and bear witness to it in unison.
Why is this? Because of great compassion of the same essence.
That which is transformed by one Buddha is the transformation of all Buddhas; that which is transformed by all Buddhas is the transformation of one Buddha.

As stated in the *Amitābha Sūtra*, Śākyamuni praises the various adornments of Sukhāvatī and further exhorts all ordinary beings to single-mindedly and exclusively recite the name of Amitābha for one day or seven days; they will certainly attain rebirth there.

The subsequent passage states: "In each of the ten directions, there are Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who together praise Śākyamuni for being able, during this age of the five turbidities, in this evil world, amidst evil sentient beings, evil views, evil afflictions, and the height of evil heterodoxy and lack of faith, to extol the name of Amitābha and exhort sentient beings to recite it, whereby they will certainly attain rebirth. This is precisely the proof.

Furthermore, the Buddhas of the ten directions, fearing that sentient beings might not believe what was spoken by the single Buddha Śākyamuni, have with one mind and at the same time each extended their tongues to cover the entire trichiliocosm and uttered these words of truth: "You sentient beings should all believe what has been spoken, praised, and realized by Śākyamuni: all ordinary people, regardless of the amount of their merit or demerit or the length of their duration—whether they practice for as long as a hundred years at most, or down to a single day or seven days—if they can single-mindedly and exclusively recite the name of Amitābha, they will certainly attain rebirth; of this there is no doubt."
"Therefore, it is indeed the case that what is taught by one Buddha is realized by all Buddhas alike.
This is called establishing faith with respect to persons.
Next, regarding establishing faith with respect to practice, there are two kinds of practice:
First is correct practice, and second is mixed practice.
Regarding correct practice: that which consists of practicing exclusively in accordance with the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* is called correct practice. What is this?
With single-minded devotion, read and recite these sutras—the *Amitābha-sūtra*, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, and the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*.
With single-minded concentration, contemplate, observe, and keep in mind the twofold adornment of that land.
If one prostrates, one should single-mindedly and exclusively prostrate to that Buddha.
If one recites the name, one should single-mindedly and exclusively recite that Buddha's name.
If one offers praise or makes offerings, one should single-mindedly and exclusively offer praise and make offerings.
This is called "right.
Furthermore, within this right practice, there are two kinds:

first, those who single-mindedly and exclusively recite the name of Amitābha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of time or duration, never abandoning it from moment to moment; this is called the karma of right concentration, for it accords with that Buddha’s vow.
If one practices recitation and so forth based on ritual propriety, these are termed "auxiliary practices" (jūgyō).
Apart from these two categories of primary and auxiliary practices, all other various forms of goodness are termed "miscellaneous practices" (zagyō).

If one cultivates the aforementioned two practices—the primary and the auxiliary—and the mind constantly remains close to them through uninterrupted mindfulness, this is called "uninterrupted" (*nirantara*).

If one performs the subsequent mixed practices, the mind will be constantly interrupted; although one may still attain rebirth through dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), these are termed "distant and miscellaneous" practices.
Therefore, it is called the "deep mind.
Third is the "mind of dedication and aspiration. Regarding the mind of dedication and aspiration:

it refers to dedicating all roots of goodness—both mundane and supramundane—cultivated through the body, speech, and mind in past and present lives, as well as rejoicing in all mundane and supramundane roots of goodness cultivated by the body, speech, and mind of all ordinary and noble beings, others; and with these roots of goodness cultivated by oneself and others, sincerely dedicating them from within a heart of deep faith to aspire for rebirth in that land. Therefore, it is called the "mind of dedication and aspiration."

Furthermore, regarding those who dedicate their merit and make vows with the aspiration to be reborn, they must, within a mind of definitive reality, perform the dedication while maintaining the thought that they will indeed attain rebirth. This mind of deep faith must be like a vajra, remaining unshakable and indestructible by any heterodox views, other schools, or practitioners of divergent interpretations and practices. It must be a single-minded, resolute, and upright advancement. One must not, upon hearing the words of such people, give rise to thoughts of advancing or retreating, becoming timid or weak, looking back, or falling from the path; for to do so would mean losing the great benefit of rebirth in the Pure Land.
Question:

"If there are those with differing understandings and practices, such as heterodox and confused people, who come to cause confusion and delusion, or raise various doubts and difficulties, claiming that one cannot attain rebirth [in the Pure Land],"
Some say:

"All of you sentient beings, from the beginningless kalpas of the past until this present life, have through the actions of body, speech, and mind committed all manner of offenses against the bodies of both ordinary beings and sages—namely, the ten evil deeds, the five heinous crimes, the four grave offenses, slandering the Dharma, being icchantikas, breaking the precepts, and destroying right view—and have not yet been able to exhaustively eliminate them."

Yet, while these offenses bind one to the evil realms within the three worlds, how is it that by practicing merit and reciting the Buddha's name for a single lifetime, one immediately enters that stainless, non-arising land and forever attains the stage of non-retrogression?

He replied: "The Buddha's teachings and practices exceed the sands of the Ganges in number; they accord with the capacities and conditions of those who receive them, and thus vary according to individual dispositions.

For example, among the things in the world that can be seen and trusted by the human eye: light can dispel darkness, space can contain all things, earth can support and nourish, water can generate and moisten, and fire can bring about both formation and destruction. Such matters are all phenomena of relative dependence (*pratītyasamutpāda*); they are visible to the eyes and differ in a thousand ways and ten thousand variations. How much more so, then, must there be manifold benefits from the inconceivable power of the Buddha-dharma?"
To exit through one gate is to exit through the gate of a single affliction;
to enter through one gate is to enter the gate of a single wisdom of liberation.
For this reason, we act in accordance with our respective conditions, each seeking liberation.
Why do you take these essential practices that lack a karmic affinity for me and cause me such confusion?
Indeed, what I cherish is precisely the practice with which I have a karmic affinity; it is not that which you seek.
That which you love is precisely that which constitutes your own conditioned practice, and it is not what I seek.
Therefore, those who cultivate their respective practices according to what they find pleasing will surely attain liberation swiftly.

The practitioner should know that if one wishes to study and understand, one may learn all things without obstruction, from the state of an ordinary person up to the level of a sage and even the fruit of Buddhahood.
If one wishes to practice, one must rely on dharmas with which one has a karmic affinity; by applying little effort, one will gain great benefit.

Furthermore, he addressed all those who aspire to be reborn [in the Pure Land], saying: "I shall now provide one more analogy for practitioners to protect their faith, in order to guard against the difficulties posed by external evils and heterodox views."
What are these? For example, suppose there is a person who wishes to travel westward for hundreds of thousands of li, and suddenly on the way he sees two rivers:
one is a river of fire to the south, and the other is a river of water to the north.
The two rivers are each one hundred paces wide and bottomlessly deep, extending boundlessly to the south and north.

Exactly between the water and fire lies a white path, approximately four or five inches wide; this path runs from the eastern bank to the western bank, also measuring one hundred paces in length. The waves of the water cross over and dampen the path, while the flames of the fire also come to burn it; the water and fire alternate in their assault without ever ceasing.

Once this person had reached a desolate and remote place where there were no other people, but many bands of bandits and fierce beasts, they saw him alone and vied with one another to come and kill him.
This person, terrified of death, ran straight toward the west and suddenly saw this great river. He thought to himself:
"I see no boundaries to this river from north to south; in its midst there is a white path, yet it is extremely narrow. Although the two banks are close together, by what means can one cross?"
"Today my death is certain; there is no doubt.

Just as he was about to turn back, the bandits and fierce beasts gradually closed in on him. When he sought to flee toward the south or north, the beasts and venomous insects vied with one another to charge at him. When he sought to find a path toward the west, he feared falling into these two rivers of water and fire. At that moment, his terror and panic were beyond description.
He then thought to himself:
"Whether I turn back now, I shall die; whether I stay, I shall die; whether I go forward, I shall die.
Since death is inevitable in any case, I would rather follow this path and proceed ahead. Since this path exists, I must surely be able to cross over."
While he was thinking this, a voice from the eastern bank suddenly called out in encouragement:
"O virtuous one, simply proceed resolutely along this path; there will certainly be no danger of death, whereas if you stay, you will die."
Furthermore, from the western bank, someone called out, saying:
"Come straight forward with single-minded right mindfulness; I can protect you, so that the multitude shall not fear falling into the calamities of water or fire."

Having heard this command to summon him, the person immediately rectifies his body and mind, resolutely seeks the Way, and proceeds straight forward, giving rise to no doubt, fear, or thought of retreat.
As he traveled for one or two *yojanas*, a band of thieves on the eastern bank called out to him, saying:
"Virtuous one, please turn back! This path is perilous and impassable; you will certainly die, there is no doubt. We have no ill intent toward you."

Although this person heard the call, he did not look back; with single-minded resolve, he proceeded straight ahead, mindful of the Way, and in a brief moment reached the western bank, forever freed from all perils.
When good friends meet, their joy and delight are inexhaustible;
this is the analogy.
Next is the application of the analogy.
The "eastern bank" is a metaphor for this Saha world, the burning house.
The "western bank" is a metaphor for the precious land of Ultimate Bliss.

The "multitude of bandits and fierce beasts feigning intimacy" is a metaphor for the sentient beings' six sense organs, six consciousnesses, and six sense objects, as well as the five aggregates and the four great elements.
The mention of a desolate wilderness devoid of people is a metaphor for constantly following evil associates and failing to encounter true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
The mention of the two rivers of water and fire is a metaphor for the craving of sentient beings, which is like water, and their hatred and resentment, which is like fire.

The statement regarding the intermediate white path of four or five inches is a metaphor for the pure vow to seek rebirth that can arise within the afflictions of greed and hatred possessed by sentient beings.
It is because greed and hatred are so powerful that they are likened to water and fire.
Because the wholesome mind is subtle, it is likened to a white path.
Furthermore, the fact that the path is constantly moistened by the waves of water is a metaphor for the constant arising of attachment, which is able to defile the wholesome mind.
Furthermore, the constant burning of the path by flames is a metaphor for the mind of anger and resentment, which can incinerate the wealth of the Dharma—namely, merit.
As for the statement that a person walks upon the path heading directly west, this is a metaphor for turning all karmic activities toward the Western Quarter.

The statement that "on the eastern bank one hears the sound of people's voices, urging one to seek the path and proceed directly west" is a metaphor for the fact that although Śākyamuni has already passed into extinction and people no longer see him, there are still the teachings to be sought; this is likened to the sound.

The mention of "one part or two parts of speech or conduct" and being called back by a band of thieves and the like is a metaphor for those with divergent interpretations and divergent practices who hold evil views; it refers to their falsely proclaiming their own views to mutually delude one another, as well as their own commission of transgressions and subsequent decline.
The mention of someone calling out from the western bank is a metaphor for the vow of Amitābha.

The mention of arriving at the western bank in an instant and joyfully meeting a virtuous friend is a metaphor for sentient beings who have long been submerged in birth and death, wandering through kalpas in delusion and self-entanglement, with no means of liberation.
I have looked up with gratitude to Śākyamuni, who dispatched me toward the West, and have relied upon Amitābha’s compassionate heart to summon me.

Now, in faithful obedience to the intentions of these two Honored Ones, I disregard the two rivers of water and fire; with every thought and without omission, I ride upon the path of their vow-power. After I cast off this life, may I attain birth in that land and behold the Buddha—how could my joy and celebration be anything less than infinite?

Furthermore, for all practitioners, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, and in whatever they cultivate through the three karmas, regardless of day or night or the specific time, they constantly maintain this understanding and constantly maintain this contemplation; therefore, it is called the mind of dedication and aspiration.

Furthermore, regarding what is called "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*): having been born in that land, one again gives rise to great compassion and dedicates oneself back into the cycle of birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings; this is also termed "dedication."
Once these three minds are fully possessed, there is no practice that cannot be accomplished.
It is impossible for one whose vows and practices are perfected not to give rise [to the bodhicitta].
Furthermore, it should be understood that these three minds also comprehensively encompass the meaning of meditative goodness (*samādhi-kuśala*).
Five: From "Furthermore, there are three kinds of sentient beings" onwards, it correctly clarifies the selection of those capable of upholding the Dharma and practicing according to the teachings.
Six: From "What are the three? onwards, up to the section on the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), it correctly clarifies the differences in how they receive the Dharma.
There are three such [points].
First, it clarifies that one should not kill out of a compassionate heart.
Now, there are many types of karmic acts of killing: there may be killing by speech, killing by body, or killing by mind.
Regarding "killing by speech," giving instructions or granting permission is termed killing by speech.
Regarding "killing by body," moving the hands or body and directing others is termed killing by body.
Regarding "killing by the mind," the act of contemplating, devising means, and calculating [the act] is termed killing by the mind.
As for the karmic act of killing itself, it does not distinguish between the four modes of birth; all such acts can incur the obstacle of sin yet still enable one to be born in the Pure Land.
To simply give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all living beings is itself to bestow life and peace upon all sentient beings; it is also the most supreme and wondrous precept.
This corresponds to the third phrase of the first merit mentioned above, which states: "to refrain from killing with a compassionate heart.
Thus, there are two types of goodness: that of restraint (*saṃvara*) and that of practice (*caryā*).
Refraining from killing oneself is called the goodness of restraint; teaching others not to kill is called the goodness of practice.
The initial severance of both self and other is called the goodness of cessation (*śamatha-kuśala*); their ultimate and permanent elimination is called the goodness of practice (*caryā-kuśala*).
Although there are these two types of goodness—cessation and maintenance—they are collectively summarized as the lower practices of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Regarding the statement "possessing all precepts and practices": if this refers to those who are vessels for humans, devas, or the two vehicles, it is called the "lesser precepts"; if it refers to those with the great mind and great practices, it is called the "Bodhisattva precepts."

If this precept is categorized by way of stages, that which corresponds to the three levels of the superior class is termed the Bodhisattva Precepts; because the stage of the person is fixed, it naturally transforms [into them], and thus it accords with the second section on the "Precepts of Merit" regarding the cultivation of roots of goodness.

Upon hearing this teaching, their minds remain composed and tranquil, giving rise to neither doubt nor obstruction.

The three types of clear knowledge involve deep faith in the two kinds of causes and effects—suffering and happiness—both mundane and supramundane. One must not give rise to doubt or slander regarding these causes and effects or their underlying principles.

If one has deep faith in the suffering of birth and death, sinful karma will never again be committed.
If one has deep faith in the unconditioned bliss of the Pure Land, once a virtuous mind is aroused, it shall never again be lost.

Second, although one's clear faith may be intermittent, one must not harbor doubt or slander regarding any aspect of the Mahāyāna; for if one should give rise to such doubt or slander, even if a thousand Buddhas were to surround one's body, there would be no means by which they could save one.

The various virtues mentioned above, including the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*), may likewise appear to be effortless; yet, it is solely by giving rise to a single thought of weariness with suffering and a desire to be born within the realm of all Buddhas that one swiftly fulfills the great compassionate vows and practices of a Bodhisattva, returning to the cycle of birth and death to universally deliver sentient beings—therefore, this is called "arousing the bodhicitta."
This meaning has already been clarified within the third section on merit.

Together with the four formless attainments and the attainment of cessation, these constitute eight liberations in total.
